about: The wrong sentences of every lesson script, by node, as canonical keys with the lesson's reason. Derived from content/scripts by npm run pitfalls and checked by the gate. Never edited by hand.

g:absolute-constructions: una vez terminar la reunión todos se fueron||
Almost. After *una vez* Spanish wants the participle, which agrees with *reunión*.
una vez aprobado la propuesta comenzarán las obras||
Almost. The participle is an adjective here, so it matches *propuesta*.
una vez que aprobado el plan comenzarán las obras||
Almost. *Una vez que* needs a full verb; with a participle, leave *que* out.
g:acabar-de-ya-todavia: Almost. *Acabo de* carries the time; the second verb is always the infinitive.
Close. You need the little *de*: *acabo de llegar*.
Nearly. For just happened, *acabar* stays in the present; *acabé de* means I finished doing something.
Careful. Not yet is *todavía no*; *ya no* means not any more.
English puts any more at the end; Spanish says *ya no* before the verb.
g:adjective-agreement: Almost. The word follows Vale, not you: she's a woman, so *cansada*.
In Spanish the *s* travels: more than one customer, so *contentos*.
*Excelente* ends in *e*, so it never changes for a woman.
g:adverbs-mente: Almost. Build it on the feminine form: *tranquila*, then *-mente*.
Well is *bien*, and badly is *mal*; good and bad don't take *-mente*.
To describe a person, use the adjective; *-mente* is for how someone does something.
g:agreement-tricky: Almost. English "people" is plural, but *la gente* is singular in Spanish.
los mayoría de los vecinos votó en contra||
Almost. *Mayoría* is a feminine noun, so it takes *la*.
la mayoría de la gente quieren café||
Almost. With *la gente* after *de*, nothing in the phrase is plural, so the verb stays singular.
g:argument-markers: no solo es barato pero práctico||también
Almost. After *no solo*, the "but also" half uses *sino*, not *pero*.
es cierto que el plan es caro y es justo||
Almost. A concession needs *pero* to turn the argument.
es cierto que el plan sea caro pero es justo||
Almost. You are admitting a fact, so use the indicative, not the subjunctive.
en el cambio nos queremos quedar|nosotros|
Almost. *En cambio* has no article. It can open the sentence or sit right after the thing you contrast.
g:article-uses: Almost. Coffee in general needs *el* in Spanish, even though English drops the.
After *soy*, the job stands alone, no *un*.
Dogs in general take *los* after *me gustan*.
With *el*, it's one particular coffee; for coffee as a habit, leave it out.
g:aunque-indicative: aunque es caro pero lo compro||
Almost. In English you'd never say although it's expensive, but I buy it; Spanish doesn't either. One connector is enough.
Rain isn't why you walk; it's what you walk in spite of, so *aunque*.
incluso aunque es caro lo compro||
Even though is just *aunque*; you don't need a separate word for even.
g:cada-cualquier: *Cada* points at one at a time, so the noun stays singular. The exception is a number: *cada dos días*, *cada ocho horas*.
Almost. Before a noun, *cualquiera* loses its -a.
Nothing follows it, so it keeps the -a: *cualquiera*.
*Cada* never takes an article. Use *todos los días* if you want one.
g:causal-advanced: lo despidieron por que llegó tarde||
Almost. *Por* takes the dictionary form: *por llegar*. With a full sentence you need *porque*, written as one word.
Unlike English *for arriving*, Spanish uses the infinitive after *por*, never the *-ando* form.
cerramos el café por nadie vino||
*Por* takes a noun or an *-r* verb. With a full sentence, use *porque*, *ya que* or *puesto que*.
*Por* looks back at a cause; for a goal you aim at, *para* comes next.
g:cause-result: Almost. *Como* only works at the front; when the reason comes second, use *porque*.
Why, the question, is two words with an accent: *por qué*.
So is *así que*; *así* on its own means like this.
g:cleft-focus: fue vale que encontró la carta||
Almost. After a person the careful choice is *quien*, which points straight back at Vale.
fueron los vecinos quien firmó la carta||
Almost. Once the highlight is plural, *quienes* and the verb are plural too.
Almost. To say "what" at the start, Spanish needs *lo que*, not a bare *que*.
lo que no entiendo es porque||
Almost. "Why" as a question is two words, with an accent on *qué*.
g:commands-tu: Almost. *Tomas* means "you take"; the instruction drops the *s*.
*Hace* is "he makes". To a friend, the instruction is *haz*.
*Seguir* changes its middle to *i*, and the command keeps it: *sigue*.
g:commands-usted: Almost. *Toma* is how you'd tell a friend; for *usted* the vowel swaps to *e*.
Odd verbs build from the I form, *salgo*, so it's *salga*.
More than one person needs the *n*.
Spanish doesn't write *z* before *e*, so *cruzar* gives *cruce*.
g:commands-with-pronouns: Almost. In a do-it command the little word goes on the end, not in front.
The little words glue on as one word, and the extra syllable needs the accent.
*Le* can't sit before *lo*; it turns into *se*.
g:como-si: habla como si es el dueño||
Almost. English can say *as if he is*, but after *como si* Spanish always uses the *ra* form.
habla como si sería el dueño||
The *would* form never follows *como si*; this spot takes the *ra* form.
Keep both words: *como si* together means *as if*, and *como* alone only means *like*.
*Como si nada* is a complete phrase, so you do not add a verb in the plain past.
g:comparative-advanced-c1: el más lo pienso el menos lo entiendo||
Almost. Spanish has no "the… the…": the first half starts with *cuanto*, the second just repeats *más* or *menos*.
Almost. *Ni que* mocks something untrue, so the verb is in the past subjunctive, not the plain present.
Almost. Advice after *más vale que* needs the subjunctive, *llegues*.
g:comparatives-advanced: Almost. English repeats "more and more", but Spanish uses *cada vez más*.
mientras más trabajo el menos duermo||
Spanish doesn't add "the"; the second half just starts with *menos*.
In this pattern *más* comes right after *mientras*, before the verb.
g:comparatives: bogotá es más fría de medellín||
Almost. When you compare two things, than is *que*.
este café es más bueno que el otro||
Spanish has its own word for better: *mejor*.
tomás no es tan alto que su papá||
mi hermana es más alta que mí||
After *que*, Spanish uses *yo*, even where English says me.
g:concession-despite: Almost. The *de* is part of the phrase, so it never drops out.
Almost. Before a conjugated verb you need *que*: *a pesar de que llueve*. Before an infinitive, no *que*: *a pesar de estar cansado*.
es caro pero sin embargo vale la pena||
*Sin embargo* already means "but", so adding *pero* says it twice.
a pesar de que el café pierde plata pero tomás no quiere vender||
The opening phrase already carries the contrast, so there is no *pero* in the second half.
g:concessive-advanced: por muy que insistas no voy a ir||
Almost. *Muy* needs an adjective right after it; before a verb you use *mucho*.
por mucho rico que sea no lo puede comprar todo||
Almost. Before an adjective like *rico*, use *muy*.
si bien el plan sea ambicioso es viable||
Almost. You accept that the plan is ambitious, so *si bien* takes the ordinary form.
si bien el plan es ambicioso pero es viable||
Almost. *Si bien* already does the job of "although", so you drop *pero*.
g:conditional-advanced: como no llegas a tiempo nos vamos sin ti||
Almost. A warning with *como* needs the subjunctive: *llegues*. With *llegas*, *como* sounds like "since".
si haberlo sabido no habría venido||
Almost. *Si* does not go before the infinitive; this one starts with *de*.
te presto el carro con tal de que me lo devuelves||hoy
Almost. After *con tal de que* the verb is in the subjunctive.
abrimos a no ser que llueve mucho||mañana
Almost. *A no ser que* always takes the subjunctive: *llueva*.
g:conditional-past-guess: Almost. The future guesses about now; for a past moment use the *-ían* ending.
Almost. *Tener* shortens to *tendr-* before the ending, just as in the future.
g:conditional-perfect: Almost. After *habría* you need the participle (*dicho*), not the infinitive (*decir*).
Close. A few verbs have their own participle: *hecho*, *dicho*, *escrito*, *visto*.
Pronouns like *lo* go before *habría*; they never slip in between.
Almost. *Había* means "had"; for "would have" you need *habría*.
g:conditional-rumour: según el diario la empresa habrá pagado sobornos||
Almost. *Habrá pagado* is you guessing, while *habría pagado* passes on what the source says.
según el diario la empresa pagaría sobornos||el_año_pasado
For something that already happened, you need the conditional perfect.
vi que el alcalde habría firmado el contrato|yo|
If you saw it yourself, you vouch for it, so use the plain past.
g:conditional: Almost. *Poder* shortens to *podr-*, just like *podré* in the future.
*Hacer* is one of the short ones: *haría*.
cuando era niño iría al parque los domingos||
Would for an old habit means used to, and that's the past habit form: *iba*.
g:consecutive-advanced: no hubo acuerdo de ahí que la reunión se aplazó||
Almost. *De ahí que* always needs the subjunctive, even for something that really happened.
no tengo la contraseña de ahí que no puedo entrar||
Almost. After *de ahí que* the present needs *pueda*, not *puedo*.
hubo mucho ruido de ahí no se oyera la pregunta||
Almost. The *que* is part of the connector: *de ahí que*.
g:consequence-connectors: English can drop "that", but Spanish keeps *que* every time.
había tan gente que no había mesas||
Before a noun use *tanto* and match it; *tan* is only for adjectives and adverbs.
es tanto caro que no lo compro||
*Caro* describes, so it takes the short form *tan*.
llovió mucho de modo nos quedamos en casa||
*De modo que* is one block, and the *que* cannot go missing.
g:cuando-indicative: cuando fui niño vivía en toronto||
Almost. *Cuando era niño* sets the scene, so *era*. It isn't about length: *Hernando fue taxista cuarenta años* wraps forty years up as one finished thing.
mientras cociné hernando lavó los platos||
*Mientras* sets the scene, so here it wants the describing past: *cocinaba*. The other side can be either: *Mientras yo cocinaba, sonó el celular.*
que llovía mi abuela hace chocolate||siempre
Keep both sides in the same time: an old habit is *llovía* and *hacía*.
g:cuyo-relatives: conozco a una mujer que su hijo trabaja en la alcaldía||
Almost. People do say *que su* in chat, but in writing *cuyo* does that job.
conozco a una mujer cuya hijos trabajan aquí||
Almost. *Cuyo* agrees with what is owned (*hijos*), not with the owner (*mujer*).
el edificio cuyos los dueños viven en miami será vendido||
Almost. *Cuyo* already does the job of *los*, so no article follows it.
Almost. *Cuyo* never asks a question; for "whose is it?" use *de quién*.
g:deber-modal: Almost. For advice, leave out the *de*. It belongs to guesses.
*Debe de* is a guess: he probably rests. For "he should rest", use *debería*.
*No* goes before *deber*, not before the second verb.
*Deber* goes straight into the next verb, with no word like *a* in between.
g:demonstratives: It's *la llave*, so the pointing word is feminine: *esas*.
*Ese* already does the job of *el*, so drop the article.
*Eso* never goes before a noun. When you name the thing, use *ese* or *esa*.
g:diminutives: Not wrong, but *momentico* sounds more local: in Colombia a word ending in *-to* usually takes *-ico*.
Drop the last vowel first, and keep the *k* sound with *qu*: *poquito*.
The ending follows the word: *casa* is an *-a* word, so *-ita*.
g:direct-objects: Almost. Unlike English, the little word goes before the verb.
el celular la dejé en la mesa||
*Celular* is an *el* word, so it's *lo*, whatever English thinks of phones.
Close. When a person receives the action, Spanish puts *a* before them.
*No* always comes first, before the little word.
g:discourse-structure: en primero lugar el local es nuestro||
Almost. *Primero* shortens to *primer* in front of a masculine noun, and *lugar* is one.
por un lado es caro en la otra mano es bonito||
Spanish has no hand here. The second side is *por otro lado*, or just *por otro*.
además de el barrio nos apoya||
On its own, to add a point, it is just *además*. *Además de* needs something after it.
g:double-pronouns: Almost. The person comes first, then the thing: *te lo*.
*Le* can't sit in front of *lo*; it turns into *se*.
g:emphatic-structures: Almost. This *si* is not "yes", so it has no accent.
Almost. To repeat the question you were asked, Spanish needs *que* before *si*.
que si me gusta qué va me encanta||
Almost. *Qué va* rejects what was just said, and here you are saying yes to it.
g:estar-gerund: Almost. The -ing form always goes with *estar*, never *ser*.
*Comer* is an *-er* verb, so it takes *-iendo*: *comiendo*.
Plans take the plain present, not the -ing form.
g:estar-location-states: el café es en la candelaria||
Almost. *Es* tells you what something is. For where it is, Spanish uses *está*.
How you are today takes *estar*: *estoy bien*.
Without the accent, *esta* means this. The verb is *está*.
g:estar-participle: Almost. After *estar*, the word agrees like any describing word: *la puerta*, so *cerrada*.
Closed is the state it's in right now, so *está*.
*Estamos* is more than one person, so the ending goes plural too.
*Cerrando* is closing, an action going on. For the state, use *cerrada*.
g:evaluative-adverbs: Almost. *Lamentable* describes a thing; to comment on the whole sentence you need *-mente*.
Luckily is a fixed phrase: *por suerte*, never *en suerte*.
*Afortunado* describes a person; the comment on what happened is *afortunadamente*.
*Lamentable* already ends in *e*, so *-mente* goes straight on.
g:exclamations: English says what a surprise, but Spanish drops the a.
*Cuánto* matches the thing, and *gente* is a *la* word.
The verb comes right after *qué bien*; the person goes to the end.
g:formal-letter-grammar: le agradecería que me responde antes del viernes||
Almost. A polite request in writing needs the past *-ra* form, not the present.
Almost. *Dirigirse* needs *a* before the person you are writing to.
te agradecería que me respondieras antes del viernes||
Almost. A formal letter uses *usted*, so *le* and *respondiera*.
escribo a ustedes para presentar una queja||
Almost. *Escribo a* is correct but too plain; letters open with *me dirijo a*.
g:future-conjecture: Almost. *Tener* is one of the short ones: *tendrá*, never *tenerá*.
Hours are plural, like *son las once*, so the guess is *serán*.
hará unas 20 personas en el parque||
*Hará* comes from *hacer*. The guess form of *hay* is *habrá*.
g:future-perfect: Almost. The last word never changes for gender or number after *haber*.
This form is for guessing or for a deadline, not for saying what you know happened.
g:future-promises: Almost. *Tener* shortens to *tendr-* before the ending, just as when you were guessing.
The accent is part of the ending: *-ré*, stressed at the very end.
*Hacer* is one of the short ones: *hará*.
After *voy a* the verb stays in its dictionary form. It's one future or the other, never both.
g:future-subj-recognition: el que no cumpliere fue sancionado||
Almost. This form looks ahead, so what follows is in the future.
adonde fuiste haz lo que viste||
*Fueres* is not the past *fuiste*: it means "wherever you may go".
No one talks this way. In conversation, use the plain present.
g:gender-articles: Feminine, but *el* before a stressed *a-* sound. The plural goes back to *las aguas*.
Words ending in a consonant give no clue; *país* is masculine.
*Ciudad* is feminine, so the plural is *unas* or *las*.
g:gerund-ways: nadando es bueno para la salud||
Almost. English uses -ing as a thing; Spanish uses the dictionary form, *nadar*.
Don't translate by: the *-ando* / *-iendo* form already means it.
After *me gusta*, the action is a thing you like, so it's the dictionary form.
No *a* before the *-ando* form. *Va a* goes with *mejorar* and means going to.
g:gustar-basic: *Yo gusto* means 'I am pleasing'. The coffee does the pleasing, so: *me gusta*.
*Gusto* is about you. The verb follows the coffee: *gusta*.
Activities always take *gusta*, however many there are.
Things you like in general keep *el* or *la* in Spanish.
g:gustar-full: Almost. Vale isn't doing the pleasing, the cake is: so *a Vale le gusta*.
The *le* has to stay, even when you name the person.
*Gustamos* would be about us. The verb follows the coffee: *gusta*.
Several arepas, so *gustan*. *Les* is about the people, not the food.
Like *gustar*, the verb follows the ajiaco: *encanta*.
g:hace-ago: Almost. English says the time and then ago; Spanish says *hace* first, then the time.
Close. *Antes* means before or earlier; for ago, counted back from now, use *hace*.
*Hace* points at a moment that is over, so the verb goes in the past: *llegó*.
Nearly. *Hace* doesn't turn plural with years; it's always *hace*.
g:hace-que-desde: hace 3 meses que he vivido aquí||
Almost. English says have lived, but Spanish uses the present, because you still live here.
Close. For how long something has been going on, Spanish says *desde hace*, not *por*.
Not wrong, but the everyday question keeps the present: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives…?*
hace un mes que el sistema no funcionó||
It's still not working, so the verb stays in the present: *funciona*.
Nearly. *Hace* never turns plural, whatever the time.
g:hay-vs-esta: hay el banco en la calle||
Almost. *El* means you already know the bank, so say where it is with *está*.
es una panadería en la esquina||
"There is" is *hay*. *Es* says what something is, not that it's there.
no hay vale en el café||
A name is someone known, so it takes *está*: *Vale no está*.
English says "there are", but Spanish keeps *hay* for more than one. *Están* is only for banks you already know about.
g:hedging-distance: no es que dudo de ti||
Almost. After *no es que* the verb takes the subjunctive, because you are pushing the idea away.
al parecer el permiso fuera falso||
Almost. *Al parecer* just reports, so the verb stays ordinary.
al parecer que el permiso era falso||
Almost. *Al parecer* is a short opener with a comma, with no *que* after it.
supuestamente vi que altamira compró el edificio|yo|
If you saw it yourself you vouch for it, so there is nothing to hedge.
g:imperfect-habitual: Almost. *Usar* can't do the job of *used to*. The ending does it: *vivía*.
mi abuela cocinó todos los domingos||
*Cocinó* sounds like one event. For something that kept happening, use *cocinaba*.
yo vía televisión con mi abuelo||
g:imperfect-progressive: estaba cocinar cuando sonó el teléfono||
Almost. After *estaba*, use the *-ando* form, where English uses -ing.
estaba cocinando cuando estaba sonando el teléfono||
The interruption is a single moment, so it takes the event past: *sonó*.
era cocinando cuando sonó el teléfono||
The was in was cooking is always *estar*, never *ser*: *estaba cocinando*.
g:imperfect-states: Almost. In Spanish you have your years, so age is always *tener*: *tenía*.
Close. *Había* stays the same for one thing or many, just like *hay*.
*Fue* sums up an event. For what a place was like, Spanish uses *era*.
g:imperfect-subj: Almost. *Tuve* just reports something that happened; a wish needs the *ra* form.
English copies its past tense here (*I wish I had*), but Spanish needs the subjunctive, not the ordinary past.
Start from *tuvieron*, not from the infinitive: the irregular stem carries over.
g:impersonal-obligation: *No se debe* says you shouldn't; when there's simply no need, say *no hay que*.
Nothing goes between *se debe* and the infinitive.
g:impersonal-register: la gente creen que el café va a cerrar||
Almost. *La gente* looks plural in English, but in Spanish it is singular: *cree*.
se dicen que el alcalde renunció||
Almost. In *se dice que* the verb stays singular, because what follows is a whole clause.
Careful. *Dice* is one person speaking; the plural *dicen* is the rumour mill, "they say".
se cree de que fue un error||
Almost. There is no *de* before *que* here.
g:indefinites: Almost. Right before a masculine noun, *alguno* shortens to *algún*.
After the verb, *ningún* needs a *no* in front, just like *nada*.
Close. English says any documents, but Spanish keeps *ningún* and the noun singular.
*Pregunta* is feminine, so the word matches it: *alguna*.
With no noun after it, the short form isn't enough: say *ninguno*.
g:indirect-objects: Almost. Spanish puts *le* before the verb instead of to him after it.
The person you ask, tell or give to gets *le*, even when she's a woman.
los vecinos le di mi número||
More than one person receives it, so *les*.
*No* comes first, then *le*, then the verb.
g:indirect-questions: Almost. *Si* meaning "whether" has no accent; *sí* is "yes".
After a question word, Spanish puts the verb before the subject.
g:infinitive-perfect: después de haber firmar se arrepintió||
Almost. After *haber*, the verb takes its *-do* ending: *firmado*.
Almost. After *por* the verb stays in its base form: *haber*, not *he*.
Almost. *No* goes before *haber*, not after it.
g:infinitive-subject: Almost. English "cooking" ends in *-ing*, but Spanish uses the plain infinitive as the subject.
After a feeling verb like *me molesta*, Spanish wants the infinitive, not an *-ando* form.
The subject is one action, so the verb is singular, whatever comes after it.
me encanta a caminar por el barrio||
English says "love to walk", but Spanish puts the infinitive straight after *me encanta*, with no *a*.
g:ir-a-plans: The *a* is not optional: *voy a* + verb.
After *voy a* the verb stays in the dictionary form, ending in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*.
*No* goes in front of the *ir* part.
g:le-doubling: Almost. It isn't wrong grammar, but it sounds like a form; people keep *le* even when they name Vale.
*A mí* adds weight, but it never replaces *me*. Both stay.
les di la llave a vale||
Vale is one person, so *le*. Save *les* for two or more: *les di la llave a los vecinos*.
Close. When you name the person who likes something, put *a* in front: *a Vale le gusta*.
g:lo-adjective: la buena es que tenemos clientes||
Almost. For an idea rather than a noun, Spanish uses *lo*, not *la* or *el*.
Almost. In this pattern, the adjective after *lo* stays in its basic masculine form.
lo malo es no hay parqueadero||
Almost. A full clause after *es* needs *que*.
g:lo-que-intensity: Almost. English "how" before an adjective is *lo* + adjective + *que*, not *cómo*.
Almost. The *que* is the hinge that joins the adjective to the rest, so it cannot be left out.
mira lo cansado que estoy a woman speaking||
Almost. The adjective inside *lo… que* still matches the person it describes.
g:mood-choice-fine: Almost. If nobody has said it yet, you can't point to it, so it needs the subjunctive.
A finished action is a fact you can point to, so it takes the past indicative.
"Whatever you want" is nothing chosen yet, so it takes the subjunctive: *quieras*.
The reason is in the past, so the verb after *como* matches it.
g:narrative-pasts: Almost. Weather that sets the scene is background, so it takes the imperfect.
Two things going on at the same time are both background, so both take the imperfect.
estuve leyendo cuando sonó el celular||
The action that gets interrupted is background, so use the imperfect.
tomás abrió la caja que encontró y vio una carta||
He found the box before he opened it. *Había encontrado* makes that order clear.
g:negation-words: Almost. After the verb, *nada* needs a *no* in front too: two negatives, one meaning.
When *nadie* comes first, it does the job alone.
*Ningún* stays singular: not a single problem.
Agreeing with a negative takes *tampoco*; *también* is for positive ones.
g:negative-commands: Almost. *No firma* means he doesn't sign. To tell a friend not to, use the subjunctive: *no firmes*.
With *no*, the pronoun goes in front of the verb: *no lo firmes*.
The short *tú* commands (*ve*, *ven*, *di*) only work without *no*. Negative: *no vayas*.
*Te preocupas* is you worry. Don't worry swaps the vowel: *no te preocupes*.
g:nominalisation: Almost. After *la* you need the noun *firma*, not the verb *firmar*.
el llegada de yesid cambió todo||
Almost. *Llegada* is feminine, so it takes *la*.
la venta el edificio preocupa a don hernando||
Almost. The owner follows with *de*, and *de* + *el* becomes *del*.
Almost. In Spanish the noun comes first and the owner follows with *de*; there is no "Yesid's" shortcut.
g:object-pronoun-position: Almost. It goes in front of *voy* or on the end of *llamar*, never in between.
English says want to see you; Spanish glues *te* onto *ver*, or puts it before *quiero*.
On the end means one word: *llamarte*, no space.
g:ojala-past: After *ojalá* the verb is never the everyday present (*estás*); for a wish about now, use the *-ra* form.
*Tendría* is the "would" form. After *ojalá*, English "I had" is the *-ra* form: *tuviera*.
Almost. *Esté* sounds like you hope she may still show up; *estuviera* says she isn't here.
g:para-que: te dejo la llave para que abres||mañana
Almost. *Para que* always takes the subjunctive: *abras*, not *abres*.
te doy mi número para llamarme||
With the dictionary form, the caller is you. Your friend calls, so *para que me llames*.
ahorro plata para que compre un carro||
If you're the one buying, drop *que* and use the dictionary form.

g:subj-wishes: A hope isn't a fact yet, so Spanish uses the subjunctive, *guste*.
When it's your own action, drop *que* and use the dictionary form.
*Estás* is a fact; a hope takes *estés*, and the *tú* can go.
g:superlatives: es el café más viejo en el barrio||
Almost. After the most, in is *de*: *del barrio*.
es el más bueno tinto de bogotá||
Best has its own word: *el mejor*.
bogotá es la más grande ciudad de colombia||
Close. The noun comes first, then *más* and the adjective.
g:tanto-como: no hay tan gente como antes||
Almost. *Gente* is a thing, so you need *tanta*; *tan* only goes with describing words.
no hay tanto clientes como antes||
Before a thing, *tanto* matches it: *clientes* is plural, so *tantos*.
Close. *Tanto* pairs with *como*; *que* goes with *más* and *menos*.
After a verb there's no thing to match, so it stays *tanto*.
g:temporal-advanced: Almost. After *en cuanto* about the future, Spanish uses *llegue*, never the future tense.
nada más tomás llegó se fue la luz||
Almost. *Nada más* wants the infinitive, then the person.
a medida de que avanzaba la noche llegaba más gente||
The set phrase is *a medida que*, with no *de*.
una vez que terminará la obra abrimos el café||
Same rule as *en cuanto*: no future after *una vez que*, use *termine*.
g:tener-que-hay-que: Careful. *No tienes que* means you don't need to; for 'you mustn't', say *no debes*.
*Hay que* never takes a person. For I have to, say *tengo que*.
After *que*, the verb stays in the dictionary form: *trabajar*.
g:tense-modal-uses: Almost. *Quise* says you wanted something and acted; for a polite opener, use *quería*.
don hernando será en el café||
A guess still follows the usual rule: for where someone is, Spanish uses *estar*, so *estará*.
For a fixed plan, use the present. *Viajaba* would sound as if the plan has fallen through.
g:that-clauses: Almost. English can drop that; Spanish always keeps *que*.
The joining that is *que*, not *eso*. *Eso* only points at a thing.
I think so is *creo que sí*: the so becomes *que sí*.
g:time-sequence: en el principio rosa no dijo nada||
At first is *al principio*, with *al*. *En el principio* sounds like the opening of the Bible.
en el final el senador pagó||
In the end is *al final*, with *al*, never *en el*.
*Esta noche* is tonight; a night in the past is *esa noche*.
For the first step in a list, say *primero*. *Al principio* describes how things were at the start.
g:topic-fronting: Almost. A fronted thing needs its pronoun before the verb.
Almost. A fronted person with *a* still needs *le* before the verb.
Almost. The pronoun must match the thing: feminine plural, so *las*.
g:verb-infinitive: Almost. Spanish has no word for that 'to': the dictionary form already carries it.
Only the first verb changes. The second one stays in the dictionary form.
English says 'dancing is great', but Spanish uses the dictionary form for an activity.
g:verbs-of-change: Almost. *Hacerse* is for something you work toward; a blush just happens, so *ponerse*.
A job takes effort, so use *hacerse*, not *ponerse*.
Staying in a state is *quedarse*; *ponerse* is more like a quick reaction.
Fame is a status you reach over time, so *hacerse* or *volverse*; *ponerse* is for a change in how someone looks or feels.
g:verbs-prepositions: Almost. English says "on", but Spanish pairs *depender* with *de*.
Almost. English says "of", but Spanish pairs *consistir* with *en*.
se trata sobre la casa de mi abuela||
Almost. English says "count on", but Spanish pairs *contar* with *con*.
g:voseo-recognition: Don't mix them. *Vos* goes with *tenés*, and *tú* goes with *tienes*.
In your own Spanish stay with *tú* and its forms, and save *tenés* for listening.
*Sois* belongs to Spain's *vosotros* and you will not hear it in Colombia.
g:vosotros-recognition: *Vosotros* has its own verb form: *sois*. *Son* goes with *ustedes*.
*Os* always means a group. One friend gets *te*.
g:wish-exclamatives: Almost. After *si* use *hubiera*; *habría* belongs to the other half of the sentence.
Almost. After *si* the wish uses the form ending in *-ara*, not the *-ía* one.
After *hubiera* you need the participle, *sabido*, not the infinitive.
Almost. *¿Quién lo dijo?* asks who said it; the exclamation needs *hubiera dicho*.
g:word-order-style: mucho el barrio ha cambiado desde entonces||
Almost. After the front word, the verb comes next and the subject follows it.
Almost. *Poco* at the front already means "hardly". Adding *no* turns it into a double negative that Spanish does not use here.
muy ha cambiado el barrio desde entonces||
Almost. *Muy* cannot stand alone; use *mucho* when it replaces "a lot".
Almost. The verb goes right after the front word.
g:written-register-a2: Almost. The greeting matches the person reading, and Mariana is a woman.
*Querido* is for people you're close to; a stranger gets *Estimado*.
You opened with *usted*, so stay there: *su respuesta*, not *tu*.
gracias por tu comentario lo esperamos pronto||
Pick one: *lo* is formal, so *tu* has to become *su* too.
g:yo-irregular: Almost. *Tener* slips a *g* into the I form: *tengo*.
Nearly. I know needs the accent: *sé*. Without it, *se* is a different little word.
Only I is odd. For we, *hacer* is regular: *hacemos*.
p:a-cuadras-de: Almost. A distance needs *a* in front of the number.
Almost. English "from" becomes *de* before the place you measure from.
Almost. For distance Colombians count *cuadras*; a *manzana* is the whole block as an area.
p:a-cuanto-esta: Almost. For a price that moves, the question needs *a*.
Almost. The price comes with *a*, not *en*.
Almost. *Los tomates* is plural, so the verb is *están*.
p:a-eso-de: Almost. *Alrededor* needs *de* before the time, just like *a eso de*.
nos mudamos a principios del año||
Almost. After *a principios de* you don't need an article: *de año*.
Almost. Clock times keep their *las*: *las nueve*.
p:a-grandes-rasgos: en grandes rasgos la propuesta tiene 3 partes||
Almost. This phrase takes *a*, not *en*; learn it as one block.
a líneas generales el informe es positivo||
Almost. *Líneas generales* takes *en*, while *grandes rasgos* takes *a*.
Almost. After *en* you need *concreto*, not the *-mente* adverb.
p:a-gritos: Almost. To turn something down you *bajarle a* it.
Almost. Spanish doesn't put a scream, it *hits* it.
p:a-la-altura-de: me bajo en la altura de la calle 72||
Almost. The fixed phrase starts with *a*, not *en*.
gire a la altura de el semáforo||
mi casa queda a la altura la iglesia||
Almost. Keep the *de*, which English hides inside "level with".
p:a-la-vez: mientras tanto cocinaba lavaba los platos|ella yo|
Almost. *Mientras tanto* is "meanwhile", not "while". It opens the second half, after the first action is told.
hablo y escribo en el mismo tiempo||
English says "at the same time", but Spanish says *al mismo tiempo*, with *a* and *el* joined.
cocinaba a la vez lavaba los platos|ella yo|
*A la vez* can't open a new half like "meanwhile" does. That job belongs to *mientras tanto*.
p:a-lo-grande: Almost. The fixed phrase uses *a*, not *en*.
celebraron el grado por todo alto||
Almost. *Lo* is part of the fixed phrase.
Almost. Spanish doesn't turn *grande* into an adverb here, it uses the fixed phrase.
p:a-lo-largo-de-esta-charla: a lo largo esta charla veremos 3 casos||
Almost. The phrase ends in *de*: *a lo largo de*.
para cerrando les quisiera dejar una pregunta||
Almost. The fixed phrase needs *ir*: *para ir cerrando*.
antes de todo les quisiera agradecer la invitación||
Almost. The set phrase for "first of all" is *antes que nada*.
p:a-lo-largo-de: caminamos a lo largo la playa||
Almost. The frame always ends in *de* before the place.
el café está a otro lado de la calle||
It is *al otro lado*: *a* plus *el* joined, and the article stays.
llovió mucho a lo largo de el año||
p:a-mi-juicio: a mi juicio que la decisión fue precipitada||
Almost. The opener is already complete, so a comma and then the sentence.
en mi juicio la decisión fue precipitada||
Almost. The fixed phrase is *a mi juicio*, with *a*.
a mi juicio la decisión fue precipitado||
p:a-mi-modo-de-ver: en mi punto de vista el proyecto es caro||
Almost. English says "in my point of view", but Spanish uses *desde*.
según mi modo de ver el plan es justo||
Almost. The set phrase starts with *a*; *según* is for quoting someone else.
p:a-ojo: Almost. The set phrase is *al ojo*, not *con ojo*.
Almost. English "by eye" pulls you toward *por*, but the set phrase is *al ojo*.
Almost. No *de* between the phrase and the number.
p:a-partes-iguales: Almost. *Igualmente* usually means "likewise"; for shares, use the whole phrase.
las ganancias se reparten a parte igual||
Almost. Both words are plural: equal parts.
cada socio recibe una parte a partes iguales a su aporte||
Almost. A share that depends on the contribution is not equal, so it needs *en proporción a*.
p:a-primera-vista: en primera vista parece una buena idea||
Almost. English says "at first sight", and Spanish keeps that *a*, not *en*.
a la primera vista parece una buena idea||
Almost. This set phrase has no article.
a primera vista parece una buena idea y tiene problemas||
Almost. The impression needs a *pero* to turn it around.
p:a-reventar: el café estaba lleno por reventar||
Almost. The fixed phrase uses *a*, not *por*.
la maleta está lleno a reventar||
Almost. *Lleno* must agree with *maleta*, so it is *llena*.
la nevera está repleta con comida||
Almost. English says "crammed with", but *repleto* takes *de*.
p:a-ultima-hora: Almost. English likes "the", but this Spanish phrase has no article.
*Hora* is feminine, so the word before it is *última*.
p:aburrir-aburrirse: *Soy aburrido* says you are a boring person; for how you feel, use *estoy*.
Without *me* the verb means you bore other people; to get bored yourself, add *me*.
A film does not feel bored; it is boring, so *es*.
p:acabar-por-inf: acabó de aceptar la oferta meaning he ended up accepting||
*Acabar de* means "has just"; for "ended up" use *por* or a gerund.
Use *por* with an infinitive, or no *por* with a gerund, never both.
*Acabar por* hints at a struggle or a long wait; for a plain event use the ordinary form.
p:acercarse-alejarse: el carro acercó a la casa||
Almost. When the subject itself moves, Spanish adds *se*.
p:actualmente: Almost. *Actualmente* means "at the moment"; for "actually" use *en realidad*.
For "lately" Spanish has its own word: *últimamente*.
en día de hoy todo el mundo tiene celular||
The set phrase is *hoy en día*, in that order.
p:adaptarse-a: English "used to" tempts other words, but this verb always takes *a*.
The *a* stays in front of an infinitive too.
p:adelantar-aplazar: adelantamos la reunión para más tarde||
*Adelantar* always means earlier. For later, use *aplazar* or *posponer*.
aplazamos la reunión en el lunes||
The new date after these verbs comes with *para*, not *en*.
The thing you move is the object, with no *para*. Use *para* only for the new date.
p:adj-de-inf: Almost. After a noun, the adjective needs *de* before the infinitive.
este tema es difícil de explicarlo||
The topic is already the subject, so the infinitive stands alone, with no *lo*.
es difícil de explicar este tema||
When the infinitive comes first with its own object, there is no *de*; *de* belongs to the order where the thing comes first.
p:adjunto-envio: encontrará adjunto las 2 cartas de referencia||
Almost. In this frame *adjunto* is an adjective, so it matches *las cartas*.
adjunto le envío mi hoja de vida to a whole company||
Almost. A company is several people, so the Spanish says *les*.
Almost. It is understood, but in Colombia a CV is a *hoja de vida*.
p:agarrar-velocidad: el bus cogió velocidad en la bajada||
Almost. *Coger* is vulgar in some countries, so *agarró* (or *tomó*) is the safe choice.
la moto iba en toda velocidad||
The fixed phrase starts with *a*, not *en*.
el bus agarró a toda velocidad en la bajada||
Keep them apart: *agarró velocidad* is the change, *a toda velocidad* is the state.
p:agilizar-tramites: el sistema agilizó a los trámites||
Almost. *A* is for people; a process follows the verb directly.
las filas largas dificulta el trámite||
Almost. The verb agrees with the thing doing the hampering, and *filas* is plural.
Almost. Before *e*, the *z* of *agilizar* turns into *c*: *agilicé*.
p:agotarse: Almost. In Spanish the patience runs out on you, so the thing is the subject and *me* says who it happened to.
The verb matches the thing that ran out, so plural *boletas* needs *agotaron*.
English says "sold out of tickets", but in Spanish the tickets themselves run out, with no *de*.
p:aguantar-conservar-la-calma: conservé calma pese a la presión||
Almost. Spanish keeps the article here: *la calma*, where English says just "calm".
Almost. *Aguantar* takes its object directly, with no *de*.
Almost. To last "until" the end you need *hasta*.
p:ahora-bien-dicho-esto: dicho esto que la propuesta tiene cosas buenas||
Almost. *Dicho esto* is a separate opener, so it takes a comma and no *que*.
Almost. *Ahora* alone means "now"; you need *bien* to get "having said that".
después de decir esto la propuesta tiene cosas buenas||
A word-for-word "after saying this" is clumsy; *dicho esto* is the short form people use.
p:ajustarse-a: el procedimiento se ajusta con la ley||
Almost. English "comply with" tempts you to say *con*, but this verb takes *a*.
todos los socios se deben ajustar el reglamento||
Almost. The rule needs its *a*, and with *el* it becomes *al*.
el contrato ajusta a la ley||
Almost. The *se* belongs to the verb: it is *ajustarse a*.
p:al-alcance-de: está fuera de el alcance de los niños||
el celular está en mi alcance||
Almost. English "in my reach" tempts *en*, but Spanish uses *a*.
estos precios están al alcance para todos||
Almost. After *alcance* the link is *de*, not *para*.
p:al-final-en-resumen: en el final todo salió bien||
Almost. English says *in the end*, but Spanish uses *al final*.
el café está en el final de la calle||
Like *in the end*, *at the end of* a place is *al final de*, never *en el final*.
total fue un día muy largo||
For the short version, use *en resumen*; *total, que* is a casual shrug that leads into what happened.
p:al-tacto: la madera es áspero al tacto||
Almost. The adjective agrees with *madera*, which is feminine.
la tela es suave a tacto||
Almost. The fixed phrase is *al tacto*, with *al* for "to the".
la tela es suave por el tacto||
Almost. English "by touch" tempts *por*, but Spanish uses *al tacto*.
p:al-tiempo-que: los precios suben al tiempo que bajen los salarios||
Both are facts, so the verb after *al tiempo que* is a normal one, not subjunctive.
sonreía al tiempo de negar con la cabeza||
The phrase ends in *que*, and an ordinary verb follows it, not *de* plus an infinitive.
la producción aumenta a medida que cae la demanda||
*A medida que* is for two things changing together step by step; for two facts side by side, use *al tiempo que*.
p:alcanzar-a-distinguir: Almost. The small *a* is part of *alcanzar a*, and English has nothing like it.
la torre es vista de lejos||
Almost. English says "is seen"; Spanish says *se ve*.
desde aquí no distingo que es|él|
p:alegrarse-de-que: Almost. English has no *of* here, but Spanish needs *de* before *que*.
me alegro de que estás bien||
After *de que*, the verb takes the subjunctive: *estés*.
For a person, use *por*: you're happy on their behalf.
p:amable-de-su-parte: eres muy amable de tu parte||
Almost. The phrase already says "of you", so no *eres* is needed.
fue muy amable de ti venir a verme||
Almost. English "of you" is *de tu parte* in Spanish, not *de ti*.
estuvo muy amable de su parte||
Almost. Praise for an act takes *ser* (*fue*), because the kindness belongs to the act, not to a passing mood.
p:ameno-pesado: Almost. The adjective agrees with *película*, which is feminine.
Almost. *Amable* describes kind people. For a talk that is pleasant to follow, use *amena*.
p:animarse-a: Almost. After *animarse* the verb needs *a* before the infinitive.
*Me animó* says someone else encouraged you; for your own courage, use *me animé*.
p:aplazar-posponer: el vuelo tuvo un aplazamiento de 2 horas||
Almost. A delay nobody chose is a *demora* or *retraso*. *Aplazar* is for decisions.
pospuse la reunión en el lunes||
Almost. The new date follows *para*, not *en*.
posponí la reunión para el lunes||
p:apropiado-para: esa camiseta no es buena para la entrevista||
Almost. *Buena* says the quality is good; *apropiada* says it suits the moment.
este lugar no es adecuado por niños||
ese comentario estuvo fuera del lugar||
Almost. The phrase is fixed: *fuera de lugar*, with no article.
p:aproximar-cifras: Almost. English says "between thirty and forty", and so does Spanish: *entre* always pairs with *y*.
Almost. "At least" is *al menos*, but "at most" is *como máximo*, not *al máximo*.
p:aqui-ahi-alla: esa mesa de aquí está libre||
*Ese* and *ahí* belong together: both point near the person you're talking to.
la droguería está ahí muy lejos||
Almost. Far from both of you is *allá*; *ahí* is close to the other person.
Spanish flips the English order: near here is *aquí cerca*.
p:arrepentirse-de-haber: me arrepiento de no le haber dicho nada||
Almost. The pronoun joins the end of *haber*.
me arrepiento que no dije nada||
Almost. After *arrepentirse* use *de* + infinitive, not *que* + a past verb.
Almost. Spanish puts *no* first: *No debí haber ido* or *No debería haber ido*.
p:arrepentirse-de: Almost. You regret yourself, in a way: the pronoun *me* always comes with this verb.
Close. English "regret" takes its object directly, but Spanish always puts *de* first.
Not *por* or *para*: the one preposition for this verb is *de*.
p:asistir-faltar: asistí la boda de mi prima||
Almost. *Asistir* always takes *a* before the event.
asistí a mi prima con la boda||
Almost. *Asistir* means to attend; to help someone, Spanish says *ayudar*.
Almost. To miss an event, *faltar* needs *a*.
*Atender* is to serve or look after someone. To attend a meeting is *asistir a*.
p:azul-oscuro-invariable: Almost. When a shade word is added, both words stay fixed.
Almost. *Verde botella* is one label and does not take an *-s*.
Almost. Neither word agrees; the pair is invariable.
p:basta-con: Almost. A new person doing the thing needs *que* and the subjunctive, *firmes*.
Almost. *Basta de* means "enough already", a complaint; for "all you need" it is *basta con*.
Almost. Use *que* only when you follow it with a conjugated verb.
p:bien-bueno: Almost. Right before a masculine word, *bueno* loses its *o*.
For how she cooks, use *bien*; it never takes an ending.
Careful. *Estoy bueno* about yourself means you think you're hot. For I'm fine, it's *estoy bien*.
p:bien-mal-vs-bueno-malo: *Bueno* describes things. For how she speaks, use *bien*.
*Estoy bien* is I'm fine. *Estoy bueno* means you're attractive, which might not be the message.
*Bien* never describes a thing directly; the bread is *bueno*.
p:brindo-por: English "to" in a toast is *por* in Spanish, never *para*.
*Brindo* needs *por* before the people you drink to.
p:cabe-destacar: cabe destacar de que es la primera vez||
Almost. Use a plain *que*, with no *de* before it.
cabe destacar que sea la primera vez que ocurre||
You are stating a fact, so the verb is not subjunctive.
cabe destacando que el informe es preliminar||
English says "worth noting" with -ing, but after *cabe* Spanish always uses the plain *-ar* form.
p:cabe-la-posibilidad: no cabe duda de que sea la mejor opción||
Almost. When you are sure, the verb stays ordinary: *es*.
cabe la posibilidad de que tomás vende el café||
Almost. A mere chance needs the subjunctive: *venda*.
cabe duda de que es la mejor opción||
Almost. "No doubt" needs the *no*: *no cabe duda*.
p:cabe-preguntarse: cabe preguntar si la medida es justa||
Almost. The writer asks the question of themselves, so Spanish uses *preguntarse*.
cabe preguntarse que la medida es justa||
Almost. A doubt is "whether", which is *si*, not *que*.
todo apunta que el plan fracasará||
p:caber: Almost. The *yo* form is irregular: *quepo*, not *cabo*.
la mesa no cabe la cocina||
Almost. Don't drop the little word: the space needs *en* (or *por* for an opening).
The verb has to match who is fitting: for *yo* it's *quepo*, not *cabe*.
p:cada-quien: Almost. It feels plural in English, but *cada quien* takes a singular verb.
Almost. *Todos* is plural and takes *tienen*; only *cada quien* and *cada uno* take the singular.
cada uno se fue a su casa||
Almost. When the group is all women, say *cada una*.
p:caer-en-cuenta: caí cuenta de que era tarde||
Almost. The little word *en* is part of the phrase and cannot be dropped.
caí en cuenta que era tarde||
Almost. After *cuenta* you need *de que*, as with *darse cuenta de que*.
me caí en cuenta de que era tarde||
Almost. Here *caer* has no *me*: say *caí*, not *me caí* (that means "I fell down").
p:caerse-lastimarse: Almost. The *me* already says whose head, so use *la*.
Falling by accident is *caerse*, so it needs *se*.
With *hacerse daño*, the body part needs *en* and an article.
p:calidad-dudosa: Almost. Spanish does not say things "have" a quality here. They *are of* it.
los materiales son de calidad dudoso||
Almost. *Calidad* is feminine, so the adjective ends in *-a*.
Almost. English makes "good quality" a noun phrase; Spanish prefers *de buena calidad*.
p:cambiar-de-por: Almost. Switching jobs is *cambiar de trabajo*, with no *mi*.
quiero cambiar esta camisa de una más grande||
A real swap at the counter takes *por*.
p:capaz-dispuesto-a: no estoy capaz de decirle que no||
Almost. *Capaz* is used with *ser*, while *dispuesto* is used with *estar*.
Being willing is a state of mind right now, so it takes *estar*.
p:caracterizarse-por: el proyecto consiste de restaurar la fachada||
Almost. English "consists of" tempts you into *de*, but this verb takes *en*.
el comité se compone por 5 miembros||
Almost. *Se compone* takes *de*; *por* belongs with *está compuesto* and *se caracteriza*.
el edificio se caracteriza de su fachada||
Almost. The trait that makes it stand out follows *por*.
p:cargar-descargar: Almost. A battery dying is something that happens to you, so Spanish uses the accidental *se*.
*Cargar* puts something in. Getting an app onto your phone is *descargar*.
The verb matches the phone, and there is only one.
p:cargo-de-conciencia: Almost. *Sentir* here has no *me*, because the guilt is what you feel.
tengo cargo de conciencia por no haber la llamado||
Almost. The pronoun glues onto the end of *haber*.
tengo el cargo de la conciencia||
Almost. The phrase is fixed, with no articles.
p:cerca-de: If no place comes after it, drop the *de*.
p:coincidir-con-en: coincido con ti en que el problema es el transporte||
Almost. After *con*, *ti* turns into one word: *contigo*.
coincido contigo que el problema es el transporte||
Almost. English drops the preposition, but Spanish needs *en* before *que*.
Almost. *Coincidir* already means "agree", so *de acuerdo* is not added.
p:coincidir-en: coincido que hace falta más financiación||
English drops the little word, but Spanish keeps *en* every time.
no coincido contigo en que es la única opción||
Once you say you don't agree, the verb after *en que* turns subjunctive: *sea*.
coincido con ti en que hace falta más financiación||
p:colores-compuestos: A shade made of two words stays fixed, so neither word takes a plural ending.
After *de*, Spanish needs the word it describes: *forma*, *color* or *tamaño*.
Almost. For a colour, say *de color* before the colour word.
p:colour-claro-oscuro: Close. The colour comes first, then *claro*.
Almost. A colour with *claro* or *oscuro* never changes: *azul oscuro* for one shirt or ten.
People will understand *marrón*, but in Colombia brown is *café*.
p:comerse-todo: Almost. The extra *me* needs something with a clear limit, like *toda la torta*.
*Comer* is for food; coffee and other drinks use *tomar*.
*Torta* is feminine, so the limit is *toda la torta*.
p:como-cuanto-verbo: Almost. Nothing goes between *cómo* and the verb, so the subject comes after it.
Almost. With an adverb or adjective, use *qué*; *cómo* goes straight onto a verb.
Almost. Before a noun, *cuánto* agrees with it: *cosas* is feminine plural.
p:como-decia: como estuve diciendo me gustaría empezar||
Almost. You were in the middle of saying it, so it takes *estaba*, not *estuve*.
como te decía a ustedes la reunión es a las 3||
Almost. The little word already names the people: *les* for you all.
volver a lo de antes vienes o no||
Almost. To say "going back to" you need *volviendo*, not the dictionary form.
p:como-es-que: cómo es que no vengas el sábado||
Almost. After *cómo es que* you state a fact, so the verb is plain.
Almost. The question needs *a*: *a qué viene*.
cómo es que se hace un tinto||
Almost. *Cómo es que* shows surprise; to ask how to do something, use plain *cómo*.
p:como-me-entere: como me enteré de que mentiste se acabó||
Almost. *Enteré* says it already happened, so it only means since; the threat needs *entere*.
como no me devuelves la plata se acabó||
A threat points ahead, so *devuelvas* rather than *devuelves*.
si llegues tarde otra vez verás||ya
With *si* it would be *si llegas*. The sharper threat is *como* plus *llegues*.
p:como-para: no es tan grave para cancelar||
Almost. After *tan* + adjective, Spanish needs *como* before *para*.
no es tan grave como para que cancelar||
Almost. With the same person doing both things, use the infinitive and no *que*.
es suficiente grave como para cancelar||
Almost. With an adjective, say *lo suficientemente*, or use *tan*.
p:como-que-echo: cómo no vienes si lo prometiste||
Almost. Without *que* you are asking how, not repeating their words in disbelief.
cómo que no vienes sí lo prometiste||
Almost. Here *si* means "but" and has no accent; *sí* with an accent means "yes".
cómo que no vengas si lo prometiste||
Almost. They told you a fact, so you echo it as they said it: *vienes*. The subjunctive is only for echoing an order.
p:como-viene-tanto: Almost. *Porque* gives a real reason; the ironic echo needs *como*.
Keep the accent: *sí* with a mark is yes, while *si* alone is if.
p:comparto-su-punto-de-vista: comparto con su punto de vista||
Almost. English says *share with*; here the view itself is what you share, so no *con*.
comparto su punto de vista said to a close friend over coffee||
Almost. *Comparto su punto de vista* is for meetings and letters. Over coffee with a friend, it sounds like you're addressing a committee.
p:con-antelacion: Almost. English "in" tempts you, but the Spanish preposition is *con*.
Almost. To thank someone before they do it, Spanish says *de antemano*.
avísenos con posterioridad si no puede venir||
Almost. *Posterioridad* looks like "posterior" and means afterwards. For early, use *antelación*.
p:con-sin: un tinto sin el azúcar por favor||
Almost. In an order, the food after *con* or *sin* comes without *el*.
English stacks the words (a cheese arepa). Spanish names the arepa first, then adds *con queso*.
un jugo de mango con agua||
In Colombia a juice is made *en agua* or *en leche*; *con agua* sounds like you want water on the side.
p:concede-pero: Almost. A bare *pero* sounds combative; a small *ya* or *de acuerdo* first makes it a conversation.
puede que tienes razón pero lo veo distinto|yo|
Almost. *Puede que* is "maybe", so the verb takes its "maybe" form: *tengas*, not *tienes*.
no dudo el proyecto sea bueno pero es muy caro||
Almost. English can drop *that*, but Spanish keeps *que*.
p:concretar: Almost. After *necesito que*, the verb switches to *concretemos*.
tenemos que concretar sobre la fecha||
Almost. English says "be specific about", but *concretar* takes the thing directly, with no *sobre*.
Almost. "Specifically" is *en concreto* or *concretamente*; *concreto* alone is an adjective.
p:condenar: Almost. *Condenar* is for serious acts, so for coffee just say what you think.
nos parece lamentable que no se aumenta el presupuesto||
Almost. After *lamentable que* the verb takes the subjunctive, *aumente*.
Almost. A proposal is a thing, not a person, so there is no *a*.
p:confiar-en-que: confío en que todo sale bien||
Almost. You are talking about something not yet true, so the verb takes the "asking" ending.
Almost. English trusts someone directly, but Spanish trusts *en* someone: *confío en ti*.
p:conformarse-con: Almost. This verb always pairs with *con*.
me conformo con que llegas a tiempo||
Almost. After *con que*, the other person's action takes the subjunctive: *llegues*.
Almost. The *me* is part of the verb and cannot be dropped.
p:conocimiento-formal: tenemos conocimiento que se detectaron varios casos||
Almost. The phrase is *conocimiento de que*, with *de*.
desconozcemos el motivo de la decisión||
p:consistir-en: el trabajo consiste de atender a los clientes||
Almost. English says "consist of", but Spanish uses *en*.
las pruebas consiste en traducir textos||
Almost. Two tests need the plural verb *consisten*.
el trabajo consiste en atendiendo a los clientes||
Almost. After *en* Spanish uses the infinitive, not *-ando*.
p:constar-de: Almost. *Consistir* takes *en* and says what something comes down to. For what it is made of, use *constar de*.
la junta está integrada de 7 socios||
Almost. The members come after *por*, not *de*.
la junta está integrado por 7 socios||
Almost. The ending agrees with the thing: *la junta* is feminine, so *integrada*.
p:container-de: Almost. English can't drop "of" here, and Spanish can't drop *de*.
me da un vaso del jugo||
After the container, no *el*: *de jugo*, just like "a glass of juice".
necesito una media docena de huevos||
English says "half a dozen", but Spanish drops the *una*: *media docena*.
p:contar-con: cuento a tomás para el sábado||
Without *con*, the verb means to tell or to count; to rely on someone, keep *con*.
To tell a story there is no *con*; it only belongs to relying on someone.
p:contar-dos-sentidos: Almost. In the present, the stem becomes *cuent-*.
The pronoun joins the end of the command, and an accent keeps the stress.
You tell a story with *contar*, not *decir*.
p:contento-con-de: Almost. *Con* is for things and people; before an action, Spanish uses *de*.
A feeling you have right now uses *estar*, not *ser*.
vale está contento con el café||
The adjective matches the person who is happy, and Vale is a woman.
p:costar-pagar: Almost. A price is about the thing, so ask what it costs: *cuestan*.
*Costar* agrees with the thing: more than one mango, *cuestan*.
People don't cost, they pay. *Costar* is for the thing.
p:costarle: Almost. Like *gustar*, the hard thing is the subject and you come in as *me*.
Close. To name the person, add *a* and keep *le* before the verb.
An infinitive counts as one thing, so the verb stays *cuesta*.
p:cuando-basic: Both halves need a verb for a person, so *me ducho*.
p:cuantas-veces-tengo-que: cuántas veces te tengo que decir que cierras la puerta||
Almost. An order is a wish, so the verb takes the *que* form: *cierres*.
The verb is *sentarse* (to sit), so *te sientes*. *Sientas* belongs to *sentir*, to feel.
cuántas veces te tengo que decir que cerrar la puerta||
English says "to shut", but after *que* Spanish needs a conjugated verb.
p:cumplir-anos: Almost. "Turns" is *cumple*; *tiene* says how old she is already.
Almost. Age goes with *tener*: you ask how many years someone has.
Spanish does not say "I am thirty"; it says "I have thirty years".
p:cumplirse-un-sueno: A dream does not do anything; it comes true by itself, and *se* says so.
rosa se cumplió el sueño de tener un café||
Rosa is the person it happens to, so she comes in with *a* and *le*, not as the subject.
The verb agrees with the dreams, so many dreams need *cumplieron*.
p:dar-a: la terraza mira sobre el parque||
Almost. English "looks over" tempts *mira sobre*, but Spanish says the terrace *da al* park.
la ventana da en la calle||
la terraza da a el parque||
p:dar-comienzo-poner-fin: Almost. What starts needs *a* in front of it.
el acuerdo puso fin de la huelga||
Almost. It is *poner fin a*, never *de*.
Almost. *Dar comienzo* is for ceremonies and papers. With friends at the table, use *empezar*.
p:dar-en-el-clavo: diste el clavo en la cabeza||
Almost. Spanish has no "head" here, just *dar en el clavo*.
diste en el clavo de ese regalo||
Almost. What you got right follows *con*.
Almost. The *el* is part of the phrase.
p:dar-igual: Almost. The phrase works like *gustar*: the thing is the subject, so you need *me* and *da*.
Almost. The person who doesn't mind needs *a* and *le*, as in *a Hernando le gusta*.
Almost, if you meant yes to a plan. *Me da igual* says you have no opinion, and it can sound cold. *Me parece bien* says you like the idea.
p:dar-la-casualidad: se dio la casualidad que ella estaba ahí||
me di cuenta de que mi primo la conocía meaning it so happened that he knew her||
*Darse cuenta* is realising something; a coincidence is *dar la casualidad*.
se dio la casualidad de que ella esté ahí||
It reports a fact, so use the indicative, not the subjunctive.
p:dar-lugar-a: la protesta dio lugar en la plaza||
Almost. *Dar lugar a* is "give rise to"; for "take place", Spanish says *tener lugar*.
Almost. English says "gave rise" with no little word, but Spanish needs the *a*.
la crisis dio un lugar a una ola de protestas||
Almost. The phrase is fixed: *dar lugar*, with no *un* in between.
p:dar-marcha-atras: tomás dio marcha atrás de la venta||
Almost. English says "back out of", but Spanish uses *con* (or *en*).
dio una marcha atrás en su decisión||
Almost. The phrase has no article: *dar marcha atrás*.
dio atrás marcha con la reforma||
Almost. The order is fixed: *marcha atrás*.
p:dar-por-sentado: doy por sentado de que usted lo sabe||ya
Almost. English has no *de* here, and neither does Spanish: *por sentado que*.
dimos hecho que el contrato estaba firmado||
Almost. The little word *por* is part of the phrase.
Almost. A command to a friend needs *des*, not the infinitive.
p:dar-tiempo: Almost. In Spanish the time does the giving and you receive it: *me dio*.
Almost. The verb agrees with *el tiempo*, not with you.
Almost. A little *de* (or *para*) links the time to the thing you wanted to do.
p:dar-un-rodeo: tomamos un rodeo para evitar el trancón||
Almost. A detour goes with *dar*, a shortcut with *tomar* or *agarrar*.
Almost. You do not "give" a shortcut; you take it.
Almost. To mean "plainly" you need *sin*, with no detours.
p:darle-importancia: Almost. Keep the little word *le*: you give importance *to it*.
As a 'don't' to a friend, the verb takes *des*, not *das*.
After *tener* you need the noun *importancia*; *importante* is the adjective.
no le des importancia de lo que dije||
You give importance *a* something, not *de* it.
p:darse-cuenta-de: Almost. *Realizar* means to carry something out. To realise is *darse cuenta de*.
me di cuenta que era tarde||
Almost. Keep the *de* before *que*, even though English has no word there.
tomás dio cuenta de que rosa guardaba una carta||
Almost. The little *se* is part of the phrase: you can't drop it.
p:darsele-bien-mal: Almost. An infinitive counts as one thing, so *da*.
Almost. The *se* is part of the phrase. Without it, *me da* just means "gives me".
se me da bien los números||
Almost. *Los números* is plural, so the verb is *dan*.
p:darsele-bien: Almost. The skill is the thing doing the giving, and you are *me*.
se me da mal los números||
Almost. *Números* is plural, so the verb is *dan*.
Almost. *Bueno en* copies English "good at"; say *se me da bien* (or *soy bueno para*).
p:dates-years: el café abrió en el 4 de junio||
Almost. On a day is just *el*; *en* is for a month or a year on its own.
Spanish puts the day first, then *de* and the month.
p:dativo-aspectual: Almost. This *me* wants a whole, countable thing: *un pollo*, not just "chicken".
se leí el libro en una noche||
The pronoun has to match the person: I read, so *me*.
me leía el libro en una noche||
Finishing the whole book is a completed action, so it takes the preterite, *leí*.
p:days-el-lunes: No *en* with days: the article does the work.
p:de-lo-mas-adj: fue una noche de lo más divertido||
Almost. The adjective describes the night, so it takes the feminine ending.
fue una noche de la más divertida||
Almost. The frame is fixed: it is always *de lo más*.
fue una noche de lo muy divertida||
Almost. You need *más* in this frame, not *muy*.
p:de-los-ojos-azules: la chica con los ojos azules es mi prima||
Not wrong, but *de* is the natural way to pick someone out: *la chica de los ojos azules*.
la chica de los ojos es mi prima||
Everyone has eyes. The describing word, *azules*, is what picks her out, so it has to be there.
la chica de el pelo largo es mi prima||
p:de-ninguna-manera: de ninguna manera no me pienso disculpar||
Almost. *De ninguna manera* already carries the negative, so skip the extra *no*.
Almost. *Alguna* in this meaning needs *no* before the verb.
no ha llamado nadie que yo sé||
Almost. The fixed phrase uses *sepa*, not *sé*.
p:de-owner: Almost. Spanish has no 's: the thing comes first, then *de* and the owner.
*¿Quién es?* asks who someone is. For whose, start with *de*.
p:de-pronto-igual: Safer as *viene*. *De pronto* behaves like *a lo mejor*: the ordinary form is always right.
Safer as *viene*. *Igual* works like *a lo mejor*: the ordinary form is always right.
Almost. Put *de pronto* first when you mean maybe; after the verb it reads as "suddenly".
p:de-verdad-que: After *de verdad que*, the verb stays in its normal form.
cómo puedes decir que no te importe||
You are quoting what the person said, so the verb stays normal.
p:decadas-siglos: Almost. A decade number never takes an *-s* in Spanish.
se conocieron a final de los 70||
se construyó a principios de el siglo xx||
p:decidirse-atreverse-a: Almost. English "dare" needs no extra word, but *atreverse* always needs *a* before the infinitive.
Close. This verb always comes with its pronoun: *me*, *te*, *se*, *nos*.
Plain *decidir* takes no *a*; the *a* belongs to *decidirse*, which also needs its pronoun.
p:dedicarse-a: Almost. English says "in" for a line of work, but *dedicarse* always takes *a*.
Keep the *a* before a verb too, unlike English.
p:dejame-que-te-ayude: Almost. After *déjame que*, the verb takes its subjunctive, *ayude*.
Almost. *Permíteme* is for a friend; to a *señora* the command is *permítame*.
Almost. Pick either *que* plus a conjugated verb or a bare infinitive, not both.
p:dejar-de-inf: Almost. Stopping a habit is *dejar de* with the dictionary form, not a word for word *stop eating*.
Without *de*, *dejé comer* sounds like I let someone eat. Keep the *de*.
After *de*, Spanish uses the dictionary form where English uses -ing.
p:dejar-mucho-que-desear: el servicio deja mucho a desear||
Almost. The fixed piece is *que desear*, not *a desear*.
el servicio deja mucho de desear||
las sillas deja mucho que desear||
Almost. The verb agrees with what you are judging, so plural *sillas* needs *dejan*.
p:demonstratives-basic: *Esto* stands alone. Before a noun, use *este* or *esta*.
It's *el café*, so *este*. The ending follows *el* or *la*.
p:dentro-de-vs-despues: rosa se fue y dentro de 3 meses volvió||
*Dentro de* counts from now; in a past story, say *tres meses después*.
el senador no pagó y volvió||mañana
*Mañana* is always tomorrow from today. In a story it's *al día siguiente*.
Almost. For the future counted from now, Spanish uses *dentro de*.
p:depende-de: Almost. On is *de* here, and *de el* becomes *del*.
There's no it to translate; *depende* stands alone.
Keep the *de* before *si*, just as you keep on in depends on whether.
p:depender-de: Almost. *Depender* always needs *de*, and *de* plus *el* becomes *del*.
English says depends *on*, but Spanish uses *de*, never *en*.
depende si me dan el préstamo||
p:describe-with-images: mi hermano es lento como tortuga||
Almost. Spanish keeps *un* or *una* in these comparisons.
mi hermano es lento como un perro||
These comparisons are fixed: for slow, Spanish always picks the turtle.
el apartamento parece como una caja||
Almost. English says "looks like", but *parece* already means that, so no *como*.
p:desde-hasta: estoy en la oficina desde 8 hasta 5||
With *desde… hasta*, clock times keep their *las*.
For until on its own, use *hasta*. *A* only works after *de*.
p:detenerse-estar-parado: el carro se estaba parado en el semáforo||
Almost. Being stopped is a state, so drop *se* and keep *estaba parado*.
los carros estaban parado en la calle||
Almost. *Parado* agrees with the cars, so it takes the plural ending.
se paró junto a la puerta toda la tarde|ella|
Almost. For a state that lasted, use *estar parado*; *se paró* is just the moment she stopped or stood up.
p:dice-ser: Almost. Use either *que* plus a full verb, or the infinitive alone, not both.
Almost. *No* goes before the infinitive, as before any verb.
Almost. A job after *ser* drops the English "a".
p:dificil-de-inf: Almost. When the thing is the subject, Spanish needs *de* before the infinitive.
las preguntas son difícil de responder||
The adjective describes the questions, so it is plural too.
este ensayo es difícil de escribirlo||
The essay is already the subject, so no *lo* is needed after the infinitive.
p:digas-lo-que-digas: dices lo que dices voy a ir||
Almost. "No matter what" needs the *que* form, not the ordinary *dices*.
digas lo que dices voy a ir||
Both halves must match: the same verb, the same *que* form, twice.
hagas lo que hagas no le dices nada||
A negative command also takes the *que* form: *no digas*.
p:directions-cuadras: Almost. *Derecha* is right; straight on is *derecho*.
Right and left need *a la* in front: *a la derecha*, *a la izquierda*.
p:dirigirse-a: Keep the *a*: *dirigirse a* never drops it.
me dirigo a ustedes para solicitar información||
me dirijo a ustedes por solicitar información||
The purpose before a verb is *para*, so *para solicitar*.
p:disculpa-que: disculpa que no te saludé antes||
Almost. After *disculpa que* Spanish wants *haya saludado*, not the plain past.
disculpe que te moleste a esta hora||
Keep the same register: *Disculpe* goes with *lo*, not *te*.
A noun for something that happened needs no *que*: *Disculpa la demora*.
p:disponer-de: Almost. *Disponer* always needs *de* before what you have.
Almost. In this sense *contar* needs *con*, otherwise it means "count".
p:doler: Almost. After a verb, a lot is *mucho*. *Muy* only goes before a describing word: *muy fuerte*.
*Dolor* is a thing you have, so *tengo*.
Pick one shape: *me duele* (the verb) or *tengo dolor de* (the noun), never both.
p:don-dona-nombre: Almost. *Don* goes with a first name, never a surname.
Almost. *Doña* comes with *usted*, so the pronoun is *la*, not *te*.
p:duplicarse: las ventas se duplicó este año||
Almost. The verb agrees with the thing that doubled: plural *ventas*, so *duplicaron*.
la economía creció por un 3 por 100||
Almost. English says "by", but Spanish goes straight from the verb to the figure.
p:durar-durante: Almost. *Durar* takes the length directly, with no *por* and no *de*.
Careful. *¿Cuánto es?* asks how much it costs. For time, use *dura*.
mientras la película tomás no habló||
Before a noun like *la película*, during is *durante*.
p:echarse-romper-a: *Echarse a* works only with a few verbs; for ordinary actions use *ponerse a*.
The *se* goes once, on *echar*; the second verb stays in the dictionary form: *reír*.
p:echo-question: Going somewhere takes *adónde*; *dónde* is for where something is.
Almost. *Cuántos* has to agree with the *kilos*: plural.
p:el-agua-fria: Almost. The *el* is only for the sound; *agua* is still feminine, so *fría*.
Before a stressed a-, Spanish says *el*: *el agua*.
p:el-azul: Almost. Spanish has no word for one here; the article does the work.
Close. For whose it is, keep *de*: *el de Vale* is Vale's.
For what it's made of, keep *de*: *la de cuero*.
p:el-capital-la-capital: el capital de colombia es bogotá||
Almost. A city is feminine: *la capital*.
Almost. For money, *capital* is masculine, so *mucho*.
p:el-frente-la-frente: tiene una cicatriz en el frente||
Almost. The forehead is feminine: *la frente*.
A weather front is masculine: *un frente*.
The priest is *el cura*; *la cura* is the cure.
p:el-frio-que-hace: no sabes cómo frío hace afuera||
Almost. English *how cold* does not become *cómo frío*: Spanish names *el frío* and adds *que*.
Don't drop the *que*; it joins the noun to the verb.
no sabes la hambre que tengo||
*Hambre* is feminine but takes *el* in the singular, like *el agua*.
p:el-orden-la-orden: Almost. Sequence is the masculine *orden*, and it needs no article here.
Almost. A cut is *un corte*; *una corte* would be a court.
Almost. A command from a judge is feminine: *una orden*.
p:el-presente-trabajo: este papel se propone analizar el transporte público||
Almost. *Papel* is a sheet of paper; a written piece is *un escrito* or *un trabajo*.
en primer lugar se expondrán el marco teórico||
Almost. The verb agrees with what is set out, and there is only one framework.
el presente trabajo se centra la vivienda informal||
Almost. *Centrarse* always takes *en* before the topic.
p:el-que-la-que: Almost. Don't drop the article: *la que*.
prefiero la que tiene ventana el cuarto||
Almost. The article matches the dropped noun: *cuarto* is masculine, so *el que*.
vale es que hace el pan||
Almost. After *es* you still need the article: *la que*.
p:el-rojo-la-grande: Almost. A colour as a thing takes *el*: *el rojo*, where English has no word at all.
la camisa me llevo el rojo||
The noun you dropped still counts: *camisa* is a *la* word, so *la roja*.
mi color favorito es la verde||
Talking about the colour itself, not a shirt, it's always *el verde*.
p:el-suscrito: el suscrito certificamos que tomás es el dueño del café||
Almost. *El suscrito* is one person in the third person, so *certifica*.
la suscrito certifica que vale trabaja en el café||
Almost. A woman is *la suscrita*, with the *-a* ending.
hola vale el suscrito quiere un tinto||
Almost. *El suscrito* is for written documents; said aloud it sounds like a joke.
p:el-x-de-y: el bobo mi hermano olvidó las llaves||
Almost. English says "my idiot brother" with nothing in between, but Spanish needs *de* before the person.
el boba de ana olvidó las llaves||
Almost. The article and the label both match the person, and Ana is a woman.
no me hables de el tipo ese||
p:empenarse-en: por qué te empeñas a pagar tú||
por qué empeñas en pagar tú||
Almost. The verb needs its little word *te* (or *me*, *se*); without it the sentence has no one who insists.
por qué te empeñas en pagando tú||
Almost. English says "insist on paying", but after *en* Spanish uses the plain infinitive, *pagar*.
p:empezar-terminar: Almost. *Empezar* needs its little *a* before the next verb.
English says 'start working', but Spanish keeps the dictionary form: *trabajar*.
p:en-apariencia: en la apariencia todo iba bien||
Almost. This set phrase has no article.
tomás tiene cara que no durmió||
Almost. After *cara de* comes an infinitive, not a *que* clause.
Almost. English says "on the surface", and Spanish uses *en*.
p:en-comparacion-con: a diferencia de el apartamento la finca es muy luminosa||
en comparación de ayer hay menos gente||hoy
a diferencia que vale tomás cocina mal||
After *a diferencia* the little word is *de*, not *que*.
p:en-cualquier-caso: es caro es decir de todos modos es la única opción||
Almost. *Es decir* says the same thing again. To set a worry aside, use *en cualquier caso*.
Almost. The phrase is *de todos modos*, with *de* in front.
es caro y queda lejos en cualquier caso es caro y queda lejos||
The phrase leads to what matters, so give the conclusion, not the objection again.
p:en-cuanto-a: en cuanto a el horario no hay cambios||
en cuanto la comida vale se encarga||
Without the *a*, it is a different phrase ("as soon as"). Keep *en cuanto a*.
respecto su pregunta la respuesta es sí||
English "regarding" has no little word, but *respecto* always needs its *a*.
p:en-general: Almost. The phrase needs its *lo*: *por lo general*.
Almost. *En general* describes the usual case, not one particular day.
la gente del barrio son muy amables||
Almost. English says people *are*, but *la gente* is singular in Spanish: *es amable*.
p:en-gran-medida: depende en grande medida de la financiación||
Almost. *Grande* shortens to *gran* before a noun: *gran medida*.
tiene razón hasta un cierto punto||
Almost. Spanish drops the article here, with no *un* before *cierto*.
lo haremos en la medida de posible||
Almost. You need *lo* before *posible*: *de lo posible*.
p:en-la-medida-en-que: te ayudaré en la medida en que puedo||
Almost. When the extent is still open, Spanish wants the subjunctive: *pueda*.
te ayudaré en la medida de que pueda||
Almost. The phrase is *en la medida en que*, with *en*, not *de*.
te ayudaré en la media en que pueda||
p:en-lineas-generales: en línea general estoy de acuerdo pero tengo dudas||
Almost. The phrase is always plural: *líneas generales*.
en las líneas generales estoy de acuerdo pero tengo dudas||
Almost. This set phrase has no article.
en líneas generales estoy de acuerdo con la propuesta||
Almost. The phrase sounds unfinished without a *pero* that names your doubt.
p:en-mi-opinion: para mi opinión el precio es alto||
Almost. Spanish says *in* my opinion too: *en mi opinión*.
en mi opinión que el precio es alto||
Almost. No *que* after *en mi opinión*: just a comma and the sentence.
When you state your view positively, the verb is the normal one: *es*.
p:en-modo-alguno: en modo alguno no acepto esa decisión||
Almost. The phrase is already negative, so *no* is not needed.
Almost. With *momento* the word goes before: *ningún momento*.
en modo ninguno acepto esa decisión||
Almost. After *modo* the fixed phrase is *alguno*.
p:en-oferta: Almost. After *en*, Spanish drops the article.
Almost. *Rebajada* describes *la camisa*, so it must be feminine.
Almost. *Descuento* needs *de* in front of it: *un 20 % de descuento*.
p:en-relacion-con: en relación el contrato tengo una duda||
Almost. This opener needs *con* before what the letter is about.
con respecto a el contrato tengo una duda||
en atención de su solicitud le enviamos el catálogo||
Almost. The set phrase is *en atención a*.
p:en-tiempos-de: en tiempos mis abuelos no había televisión||
Almost. The frame needs *de* before the person.
en tiempos de mis abuelos no hay televisión||
It is a memory from the past, so the verb is *había*.
en tiempos de el abuelo de vale no había carros||
p:enamorarse-de: Almost. English says *with*, but Spanish always links the person with *de*.
Being in love is a state you are in, so *estoy*.
The adjective agrees with her, so it ends in *-a*.
p:encarecer-abaratar: la subida hizo el transporte caro||
Understandable, but Spanish prefers the one-word verb built from the adjective.
Almost. *Abaratar* is an *-ar* verb, so the past ends in *-ó*, not *-ió*.
Almost. The verb is *oscurecer*, with the *-ec-* in the middle.
p:encontrar-participle: Almost. The state describes the door, so it matches it: *puerta*, *abierta*.
No *estaba* here. The state sits right after the thing.
Close. *Llegamos* is more than one person, so *cansados* takes the *s*.
More than one window, so the state is plural too.
p:encontrar-ver-adj: Almost. The adjective agrees with the person you are judging: she, so *cansada*.
Almost. Use the pronoun *te* in front of the verb, not a separate *a ti*.
Almost. English puts *it* after the verb, but Spanish puts *lo* in front: *lo encuentro*.
p:encontrarse-hallarse: el director encuentra en la oficina||
Almost. Without *se*, *encuentra* means he finds something.
los documentos se encuentra en la oficina||
Almost. The verb agrees with what is located: several documents, *-n*.
el edificio se halla el centro histórico||
Almost. Like *estar*, it still needs *en* before a place.
p:enojarse-con: Almost. With *con*, *mí* fuses into one word: *conmigo*.
English says *angry at*, but Spanish uses *con* for the person.
*Con* is for people; for the reason, use *por*.
p:enredarse: hay un enredado con el pedido||
Almost. The noun for a mess is *enredo*.
p:enterarse-de: Almost. People say it, but with this verb the *de* stays before *que*.
Without *me*, the verb does not mean to find out.
English says *found out the news*, but Spanish adds *de* before the thing.
p:entiendo-que-subj: Almost. The first only reports a fact; to say her feeling makes sense, change the ending to *estés*.
Plain news about what someone does stays in the ordinary form; the subjunctive is for feelings.
entiendo que no te gusta el cambio||
To show you accept the feeling, *gusta* becomes *guste*.
p:entonces-de-repente: entonces se fue la luz sin avisar||
Almost. *Entonces* is only the next step; for something unexpected Spanish uses *de repente*.
Going to eat was the plan, not a surprise, so use *luego*.
The events of a story use the simple past, not the present.
p:entonces-quedamos: Not wrong, but *entonces* here can sound as if the eating caused the dancing. For a plain next step, *y después* is clearer.
tengo mucho trabajo porque no puedo salir||
*Porque* gives a reason, not a result. After the reason, the result needs *o sea que*.
tengo mucho trabajo tan no puedo salir||
English so has two jobs. *Tan* is only for so tired, so big. For so as a result, use *o sea que* or *así que*.
p:entrarle-algo: Almost. You are not the one who enters: the fear enters you, so the person is *me*.
Almost. *Ganas* is plural, so the verb is too.
Almost. The pronoun goes before the verb.
p:entre-las-ventajas-destaca: entre las ventajas destacan el precio||
Almost. The verb follows the one thing that stands out, not the plural list.
entre las desventajas destaca los costos||
Almost. *Los costos* is plural, so the verb is too.
en contra cabe señalar la conexión no es buena||siempre
Almost. After *cabe señalar*, a whole clause needs *que*.
p:entregar-recoger: A person as the object needs *a*, so *a los niños*.
entregué las llaves para el dueño||ya
English "to" tempts *para*, but the person who receives something takes *a* (here *al*), usually with *le* too.
*Pasar* needs *a* before the verb that says why you drop by.
p:entusiasmar-fascinar: Almost. The history does the fascinating; you are the one it fascinates, so *me*.
Almost. Like *gustar*, the verb agrees with the thing, and cars are plural.
