Almost. A feeling about someone else's action takes the subjunctive, *vengas*.
p:equivocarse-de: Almost. You still need *de* before what you got wrong.
For a mistake inside something, like a bill, it's *en*.
p:equivocarse: Being wrong is a state, so it takes *estar*.
Almost. English makes a mistake, but Spanish doesn't *hacer* one. The everyday way is *me equivoqué*.
p:es-adj-inf: Almost. No *de* here: the verb follows the describing word directly.
An activity as the subject is the dictionary form in Spanish, not the -ing form.
For it's important to, Spanish uses *es*, not *está*.
p:es-de-noche-tarde: Almost. For the time of day, Spanish uses *es*, not *está*.
Spanish needs the *de*: it's of night.
I'm late isn't *estoy tarde*: Spanish says you arrive late, *llego tarde*.
p:es-increible-como: es increíble que toca la guitarra||
Admiring the way someone does it needs *cómo*; *que* means that and brings a different verb form.
English says how to cook, but here someone actually cooks, so use a conjugated verb.
p:es-obligatorio: Almost. The infinitive follows directly, with no *de*.
no es obligatorio entrar sin cita||
*No es obligatorio* only means you don't have to; for a ban, use *está prohibido*.
After *es obligatorio* the verb stays in its infinitive form.
p:es-tiene-lleva: Almost. *Tiene* already says whose eyes they are, so Spanish just says *los ojos*.
Colours come after the thing: *una chaqueta roja*.
Hair is something she has, so *tiene*. *Es* is for what she is: *es alta*.
p:es-una-lastima-que: es una lástima que cierran el café||
Almost. After *una lástima que*, the verb takes its subjunctive: *cierren*.
No *de* here: *lástima que* goes straight into the verb.
Don't drop the *que*, or the sentence falls apart.
p:es-verdad-eso-de-que: es verdad que cierren la sede||
Almost. When you check a claim, the verb stays in its normal form.
es verdad de que van a cerrar||
No *de* here; only *eso de que* has one.
es verdad eso que van a cerrar||
The phrase is *eso de que*, with *de*.
p:eso-de-que: eso de que vaya a renunciar es puro chisme||
Almost. You are quoting what people claim, so the verb stays ordinary: *va*.
eso que va a renunciar es puro chisme||
Almost. For a claim you hold at arm's length, you need *de que*.
esa de que va a renunciar es puro chisme||
Almost. It points at a whole idea, so it is always neuter *eso*.
p:esta-claro-que: está claro que tomás tenga razón||
Almost. A fact takes the ordinary verb; the subjunctive is for when you are not sure.
no está claro que altamira compra el café||
Almost. After *no está claro que* you are doubting, so the verb takes the subjunctive.
está claro de que tomás tiene razón||
Almost. Nothing goes between *claro* and *que*: no *de*.
p:esta-prohibido-que: está prohibido que fumar en el café||
Almost. *Que* needs a verb with its own person; for the bare activity, drop *que* and keep the infinitive.
te prohíbo que me hablas así||
Almost. After *que* the verb takes the subjunctive: *hables*, not *hablas*.
Almost. A rule that holds here and now is a state, like *está cerrado*, so it takes *está*.
p:esta-prohibido: está prohibido de entrar sin cita||
Almost. Nothing goes between *prohibido* and the infinitive, so no *de*.
A ban on a notice is a state of things, so Spanish uses *está*.
To tell one person not to do something, the verb takes the command form *fumes*.
p:estallar-desencadenarse: *Explotar* is for bombs and tempers; wars and scandals *estallan*.
la amistad estalló poco a poco||
*Estallar* is only for sudden events; slow starts use *surgir* or *empezar*.
p:estar-a-favor-de: Almost. Taking a side is a position you are in, so Spanish uses *estar*.
estoy en contra que cierren la biblioteca||
Almost. *En contra* always needs its *de*, even in front of *que*.
estoy en contra de que cierran la biblioteca||
Almost. After *de que* the verb switches to the subjunctive, *cierren*.
p:estar-a-grados: Almost. English says *it is*, but Spanish gives the temperature with *estamos a* or *hace*.
Don't drop the *a*: it is the little word that points at the number.
That mixes the two frames: the *a* goes with *estamos*, not with *hace*.
p:estar-a-price: Almost. Spanish needs *a* before the price: *está a cuatro mil*.
a cómo es el kilo de tomate||
Close. Today's price is how things are right now, so it's *está*, not *es*.
Nearly. Several mangoes, so the verb is *están*.
p:estar-a: Almost. Spanish uses *a* for a figure on a scale, not *en*.
English says "two blocks from here" with nothing in front; Spanish needs *a* before the distance.
p:estar-al-tanto-de: soy al tanto de los cambios||
Almost. Being informed is a state, and states use *estar*.
estoy al tanto con los cambios||
The phrase always links to what you know with *de*.
English says "some knowledge in", but *nociones* is followed by *de*, just like *al tanto de*.
p:estar-convencido-de: Almost. Keep the *de* before *que*; leaving it out is a common slip.
no estoy seguro de que es buena idea||
Almost. When you are not sure, the verb after *que* takes the subjunctive: *sea*.
soy convencido de que dice la verdad||
p:estar-de-acuerdo-con-en: Agreeing is a state of mind, so it takes *estar*, not *ser*.
estamos de acuerdo con cambiar la fecha||
Before an action, the little word is *en*, not *con*.
p:estar-harto-de-que: estoy harta de que llegas tarde||
Almost. After *de que* the verb takes the subjunctive: *llegues*.
Almost. English likes "-ing" here, but Spanish uses the infinitive after *de*.
Almost. A feeling you are in right now takes *estar*.
p:estar-harto-de: Almost. Being fed up is how you feel right now, so Spanish uses *estar*.
Almost. Spanish needs *de* between *harto* and what you're fed up with.
p:estar-hecho-de: la mesa es hecha de madera||
Almost. With *hecho* the verb is *estar*; with just the material it's *es de*.
las sillas están hecho de metal||
*Hecho* describes the chairs, so it matches them: *hechas*.
English says 'made of wood' too, so keep the *de* before the material.
p:estar-hecho-un-desastre: mi cocina está hecho un desastre||
Almost. Keep *un*: it is "made into a disaster".
mi cuarto es hecho un desastre||
Almost. A mess is a state, so *estar*, not *ser*.
p:estar-orgulloso-de: Almost. *Soy orgulloso* describes a proud, stuck-up person; for pride in someone, use *estoy*.
The *de* stays in front of *que*, just as it stays in front of *ti*.
The adjective matches the person who feels proud, and *ella* is a woman.
p:estar-por: Almost. For an intention that is still forming, Spanish uses *por*, not *para*.
tengo pensado de viajar en diciembre||
Almost. *Tengo pensado* goes straight into the infinitive, with no *de*.
me hice propósito de aprender otro idioma||
Almost. The phrase needs its *el*: *me hice el propósito de*.
p:estar-regalado: Almost. The price is a state of things right now, so Spanish uses *estar*.
Almost. *Regalados* has to agree with the plural *mangos*.
los mangos están a precio del huevo||
Almost. The set phrase is *a precio de huevo*, with no *el*.
p:estar-seguro-de-que: soy seguro de que tiene razón||
Being sure is a state of mind, so it takes *estar*.
seguro de que hernando tiene hambre||
Without *estoy*, drop the *de*: the casual version is just *seguro que*.
estoy seguro de que tenga razón||
When you are sure, state it as a fact with the ordinary form. The subjunctive is for when you are not sure.
p:estaria-bien-que: estaría bien que salimos un día con vale||
Almost. After *estaría bien que* the next verb takes the *-ra* form, like English "if we went".
estaría bien de que saliéramos un día con vale||
Almost. *Que* comes straight after *bien*; there is no *de* in between.
sería bien que saliéramos un día con vale||
Almost. The set phrase uses *estar*: *estaría bien*, not *sería bien*.
p:estimado-colon: *Estimado* agrees with who you write to: a woman is *Estimada*.
*Querida* is for people close to you. A formal letter uses *Estimada*.
p:estrenar: The film is the thing being opened, so Spanish adds *se*.
estrené el celular por primera vez||ayer
*Estrenar* already means for the first time, so you do not say it twice.
estrenamos en el carro nuevo el domingo||
The new thing comes straight after the verb, with no *en*.
p:event-ser-en: Almost. Events happen, they don't sit anywhere, so *es*.
había un accidente en la séptima||
*Había un accidente* sets a scene: it was already there when you passed. To report that it happened, use *hubo*.
p:exclamations-basic: The word agrees with what you mean: *la casa*, so *bonita*.
English says how pretty, but Spanish reacts with *qué*, not *cómo*.
p:extranar: A person who is missed needs the little *a*.
Almost. The pronoun is the person being missed, so to say *I miss you* you need *te extraño*.
extraño a la comida de mi mamá||
The little *a* is only for people, not for food or places.
p:fabricado-con-contener: Almost. *Contiene* is for what is inside something; for the material an object is built from, use *está fabricada con*.
las sillas están fabricado con metal||
*Fabricado* is an adjective, so it agrees with *sillas*.
esta mesa es fabricada con madera||
You are describing how the table is, so Spanish uses *está*.
p:felicitaciones-por: Almost. Spanish congratulates you *por* something, not *en* it.
After *por*, use the dictionary form, not a past form.
p:fijarse-reparar-en: te fijaste el color del carro||
Almost. English drops the preposition, but Spanish keeps *en*.
Almost. *Fijarse* is reflexive, so it needs *me*.
nadie se reparó en el detalle||
Almost. *Reparar en* is not reflexive: no *se*.
p:focus-adverbs: Almost. *Incluso* says "even", as if mornings were a surprise; for your favourite moment, use *sobre todo*.
Almost. For "that's exactly why", Spanish says *precisamente por eso*.
vinieron todos sobre todo hernando que nunca sale||
Almost. A surprise is *incluso*; *sobre todo* would mean he came more than the rest.
p:formar-parte-de: formo parte de el equipo de ventas||
p:fracciones-de: la mitad los vecinos quiere vender||
Almost. A fraction always needs *de* before the group.
la mitad de el dinero es de vale||
medio de los vecinos quiere vender||
Almost. English "half" covers both, but before *de* and a group Spanish needs the noun *la mitad*.
p:frequency-scale: Almost. If *nunca* comes after the verb, put *no* before it: *No bailo nunca*, or just *Nunca bailo*.
Sometimes is just *a veces*. (*Algunas veces* works too, but *vez* is a *la* word, so never *algunos*.)
Close. When *nunca* comes first, it does the job alone; the *no* only appears when *nunca* goes after the verb.
p:fruto-fruta: Almost. For fruit you eat, use *fruta*.
es la fruta de muchos años de trabajo||
A result of work is *el fruto*.
*Leño* is one log; firewood in general is *leña*.
p:fuera-de-serie: es una fuera de serie cantante||
Almost. The phrase goes after the noun it describes.
son unos músicos fueras de series||
Almost. The phrase is fixed and never takes a plural ending.
es una pastelera de serie fuera||
Almost. The order is fixed: *fuera de serie*.
p:fuera-de-servicio: el ascensor es fuera de servicio||
Out of order is a state that can change, so *está*.
el ascensor está fuera de servicio por el lunes||
For "since" plus a time, Spanish uses *desde*, not *por*.
Without *se* it sounds like the oven damaged something else.
p:fuerte-como-un-roble: mi abuelo es fuerte como un pino||
Almost. These comparisons are fixed, so keep the standard picture: the oak.
este pan es duro como una piedra||
Almost. The bread got hard, it was not born hard, so Spanish uses *está*.
mariana es rápido como un rayo||
Almost. The adjective agrees with Mariana, so it is feminine: *rápida*.
p:gasto-inversion: *Gasto* is masculine, so *un*. *Inversión* is feminine, so *una*.
*Salir* tells how it turns out in the end. *Es* just states it.
There is no article, like "gained weight" in English.
p:generic-tu-uno: Almost. *Uno* is a third-person word, so the verb is *puede*, not the *yo* form.
cuando uno está cansado todo te molesta||
Almost. *Te* belongs with *tú*; with *uno* the matching pronoun is *le*.
p:gracias-a-por-culpa-de: gracias a el artículo todos lo saben||
por culpa a altamira perdimos el café||
The blame phrase ends in *de*, not *a*.
gracias al incendio perdimos la casa||
Losing a house is not something to thank anyone for. Blame needs *por culpa de*.
p:gracias-por: Almost. *Gracias* is a noun, so it takes *muchas*, not *muy*.
Close. After *por*, the verb stays in its dictionary form: *venir*, not *vienes*.
Nearly. English says "for" both ways, but thanks always take *por*.
p:gustar-mas-que: me gusta más el té más que el café||
Almost. *Más* appears once, right after *gusta*; *que* does the rest.
me gusta más leer que la televisión||
Keep both sides the same kind: an activity against an activity, so add *ver*.
me gusta más los perros que los gatos||
The dogs are more than one, so *gusta* becomes *gustan*.
p:habria-que-ver-si: habría que ver que es verdad||
Almost. You are asking whether, so you need *si*, not *que*.
habría que ver si sea verdad||
No subjunctive after *si*; the verb stays normal.
tendría que ver si es verdad||
*Tendría que* needs a someone; *habría que* is for nobody in particular.
p:habria-que: Almost. After *habría que* the verb stays in the infinitive, not tied to a person.
The *que* is part of the phrase, like ought to in English, so keep it.
The phrase never changes for a person: it is always *habría que*.
p:habria-sido-mejor: Almost. English says *better to wait*, but Spanish goes straight to the infinitive, with no little word.
After *que* in this frame you need the subjunctive, *hubieras esperado*, not a plain present.
qué harías si altamira hubiera comprado el café|tú|
Keep both halves in the past: *habrías hecho* with *hubiera comprado*.
p:hace-frio: Almost. Weather makes in Spanish: *hace frío*. *Es frío* describes a thing, like cold soup.
After *hace*, *frío* is a thing, so really is *mucho*.
For how your body feels, Spanish says you have cold: *tengo frío*.
p:hacer-frente-a: hizo frente la crisis con calma||
no sé cómo vamos a afrontar a estos gastos||
Almost. *Afrontar* takes its object directly, with no *a*.
tuvo que hacer frente de una deuda||
Almost. The preposition is always *a*, never *de*.
p:hacer-la-vista-gorda: el alcalde hizo las vistas gordas||
Almost. The phrase is fixed: *la vista gorda*, never plural.
las autoridades hicieron la vista gorda de los abusos||
Almost. English says "to", but Spanish uses *ante* (or *con*) here.
el alcalde hizo el ojo ciego||
Almost. English says "blind eye", but Spanish says "fat sight": *la vista gorda*.
p:haces-bien-en: haces bien de esperar a vale||
Almost. With *haces bien* the link word is *en*, not *de*.
eres bien en esperar a vale||
Almost. English says "you are right", but Spanish says "you do well", so the verb is *hacer*.
haces bien en esperando a vale||
Almost. After *en* use the plain infinitive, not an *-ing* form.
haces bien no esperar a vale||
p:hacia-las-nueve: Almost. *Hacia* replaces the *a*, so you do not need both.
Almost. Ten o'clock is plural, *las diez*; only one o'clock is *la una*.
Almost. The phrase is *a eso de*, with *de*.
p:hasta-la-coronilla: estoy hasta la cabeza de sus excusas||
Almost. The idiom is fixed: *coronilla* is the very top of the head.
estoy hasta la coronilla que me llamen||
saco de quicio que llegue tarde|yo|
Almost. The lateness does the driving, so it is the subject, and you are *me*.
p:hasta-la-fecha: hasta la momento no hay heridos||
Almost. *Momento* is masculine, so it is *el momento*.
hasta fecha no se ha encontrado al responsable||
Almost. English drops the article ("to date"), but Spanish keeps *la*.
Almost. English says "for now", but Spanish does not use *para* here: say *de momento*.
p:hasta-que-no: no me voy hasta que lo veo||
Almost. The seeing hasn't happened yet, so the verb takes the subjunctive, *vea*, not *veo*.
hasta que no me pagues empiezo||
The *no* after *hasta que* is only decoration; the real *no* belongs on the main verb, just like "I won't start until...".
hasta no me pagues no empiezo||
Keep the *que*: it is *hasta que*, and then the extra *no*.
p:hay-que-tener-en-cuenta: hay que tener en cuenta que el tráfico||
Almost. *Que* introduces a full sentence with its own verb; for just a noun, leave it out.
hay que tener en cuenta de que el presupuesto es limitado||
Spanish says *tener en cuenta que*, with no *de* in the middle.
hay que tener cuenta el tráfico||
The fixed phrase needs the *en*: *tener en cuenta*.
p:hay-varios-tipos: están varios tipos de café en colombia||
Almost. To say that something exists, Spanish uses *hay*, not *están*.
Say *el primero*, with its article, like "the first one".
hay varios clases de pan en el café||
*Clase* is feminine, so *varias*, even though *tipos* takes *varios*.
p:hedge-knowledge: Almost. Before a noun, *un poco* needs *de*.
With *nada* after the verb, Spanish also puts *no* in front.
How you do something is *bien*, not *bueno*.
p:horas-y-horas: Almost. Both words go in the plural.
he llamado he escrito y nada||
In a finished story the tries go in the plain past: *llamé*, *escribí*. *He llamado* would mean you're still trying.
p:hoy-les-voy-a-hablar: Almost. *Ir* plus infinitive always needs the little *a*: *voy a hablar*.
voy a les hablar del barrio||hoy
*Les* goes before *voy*, or is glued to the end: *voy a hablarles*. Never in the middle.
les voy a hablar de el barrio||hoy
p:humedo-mojado: Almost. Wet is how the clothes are for now, so *está*, not *es*.
For a climate or a place, use *húmedo*; *mojado* is for things that just got wet.
If you are soaked after the rain, say *empapado*; *húmedo* is much too mild.
p:imperativo-y-veras: No *si* here: the command itself plays the part of "if".
Start with a real command (*pruébalo*), not the plain *tú* form.
p:imperfecto-citativo: Almost. *Llegó* is a finished past, but *mañana* is the future; the *-aba* form is what carries reported news.
About your own plan, the *-aba* form sounds evasive, as if you don't know when you arrive.
vale estaba llegando de medellín no||mañana
Almost. English says "was arriving", but Spanish needs only the one word: *llegaba*.
p:imperfecto-cortesia-venia: vine a ver si me podían atender||
Almost. *Vine* says you came and that is over; the polite ask needs *venía*, which keeps the request open.
le quería a pedir un favor||
*Querer* takes the infinitive straight away; only *venir* needs the *a*.
le escribía a preguntar por mi solicitud||
*Escribir* takes *para* before the purpose; *venir* is the one that takes *a*.
p:imperfecto-sorpresa: Almost. The present is a neutral question; the imperfect tells your friend you are surprised.
The preterite means a finished event; for "I thought you had" use the imperfect.
The question is really a reproach, so answer the point and not the tense.
p:importar-un-comino: importo un comino lo que diga|yo|
Almost. *Importar* works like *gustar*: the thing matters *to* you, so the small word is *me*.
a hernando me importa un comino el fútbol||
Almost. The small word has to match the person who doesn't care: Hernando is *le*.
me importa una comino la plata||
Almost. *Comino* is masculine, so it is *un comino*.
p:imprescindible: Almost. *Que* needs a verb with a person; if no one is named, drop *que* and use the infinitive.
Almost. After *es imprescindible que*, the verb takes the subjunctive, never the ordinary one.
Almost. English says *for you to sign*; Spanish has no *for you* here, so use *que* and a new verb.
p:inclinado-torcido: Almost. A street that climbs steeply is *empinada*.
Almost. *Empinado* is only for slopes; a crooked picture is *torcido*.
Almost. The adjective agrees with *corbata*, which is feminine.
p:indefinites-basic: When *nada* comes after the verb, the *no* stays in front.
In a no-sentence, anything is *nada*, not *algo*.
Before the verb, *nadie* is already the no. Adding *no* is one too many.
p:indice-tasa: el número de pobreza sigue alto||
Almost. A rate or level is *índice* or *tasa*, not *número*.
un millar personas firmó la carta||
Almost. *Un millar* needs *de* before the people.
la tasa de desempleo bajó por un 2 por 100||
Almost. Spanish has no word for "by" here: the verb is followed straight by *un 2 %*.
p:inevitable: Almost. After *es inevitable que*, Spanish uses the subjunctive: *haya*.
inevitable los precios van a subir||
For "inevitably" you need the adverb ending in *-mente*.
es inevitable para los precios subir||
English says *for prices to go up*; Spanish says *que* plus the subjunctive.
p:infinitive-instructions: Almost. English says No smoking, but Spanish uses the dictionary form: *fumar*.
On a sign for everyone, use the dictionary form; *No fumes* is said to one friend.
*No* goes in front of the verb, never after it.
p:intensificadores: Almost. *Imposible* can't be a little bit true, so use *completamente* instead of *muy*.
Almost. *Muy falso* sounds weak, because *falso* is all or nothing.
p:intentar-conseguir: Almost. To end up with a thing, use *conseguir*; *intentar* needs a verb after it.
No *a* after *lograr*: it goes straight into the verb.
*Intentar* takes no *de*. Only *tratar* does: *traté de llamarte*.
p:interesado-en: Almost. *Interesado* always takes *en* in this meaning.
Almost. Being interested is a state, so *estar*. *Ser interesado* means "self-serving".
Almost. After *interesados en que*, the next verb takes the subjunctive.
p:ir-a-velocidad: voy a 60 kilómetros en una hora||
Here *rápido* is an adverb, so it doesn't agree with anyone.
p:ir-en-aumento: The small word in this phrase is always *en*.
*Ir* agrees with what is changing, and *casos* is plural.
los precios se dispararon poco a poco||
*Dispararse* means a sudden jump; for a slow change, use *ir en aumento*.
p:ir-venir: vengo a tu casa a las 6||
Moving towards the person you're talking to is *ir* in Spanish.
*Aquí* is where you are, and towards you is *venir*.
p:ironic-praise: Almost. After *qué* in an exclamation, the noun comes without *un*.
no sé qué hice sin ti||
What I would have done is *habría hecho*, the would have form.
p:jugar-a: *Jugo* is juice. The verb needs the *ue*: *juego*.
p:juraria-que: juraría que haya dejado las llaves en la mesa||
Almost. You feel sure, so the verb after *juraría que* stays ordinary.
juro que dejé las llaves en la mesa||
Almost. *Juro* is a flat oath; *juraría* leaves room to be wrong, which is what you want here.
me da la impresión que tomás no quiere vender||
Almost. After *impresión* Spanish keeps the *de* in front of *que*.
p:la-cara-que-puso: Almost. The article is what makes it an exclamation, so keep it.
Almost. *Cada* always goes with a singular noun.
Almost. Keep the article after *con*: *el frío que hace*.
p:la-gente-singular: Almost. *Gente* is one word for the crowd, so it takes *es* and a singular *amable*.
*Gente* is feminine and singular, so *mucho* becomes *mucha*.
The verb follows *gente*, which counts as one: *habla*, not *hablan*.
p:la-mayoria-de: la mayoría los clientes pide tinto||
Almost. Spanish needs *de* between *la mayoría* and the group.
el mayoría de los clientes pide tinto||
Almost. *Mayoría* is feminine, so it's always *la*.
casi todos de los clientes pagan en efectivo||
Almost. *Casi todos* goes straight to the group, with no *de*.
p:la-menor-idea: Almost. *La menor idea* needs a *no* to make the negative.
Almost. In this fixed phrase there is no *una*.
he visto algo así en mi vida||
Almost. Without *no* at the verb, it says you have seen it.
p:la-nombraron-directora: Almost. As in English "appointed director", the role takes no article.
Almost. The role matches the person, and *la* is a woman.
Almost. A named person as the object needs *a* in front.
p:la-vi-salir: Almost. Spanish uses the small word *la* before the verb, not *ella* after it.
Almost. The thing they did stays as the plain *-r* verb.
Almost. The small word goes before the whole *había visto*.
p:lamento-lo-de: lamento lo de el otro día||
Almost. You need *lo* in front of *de*: it is what means "that matter".
Almost. English needs "about", but *lo de* already does that job: no *sobre*.
p:lavarse-las-manos: Almost. *Me* already says they're yours, so *mis* says it twice.
Put the owner in the little word *me*, and give the teeth *los*.
*Se* already tells you they're Vale's own hands.
p:le-agradeceria-que: le agradecería que me envía la factura||
Almost. After *agradecería que* use the *-ra* form, not the plain present.
le agradecería que me enviaría la factura||
Almost. English says "would" twice, but only *agradecería* takes it; after *que* comes the *-ra* form, *enviara*.
le agradecería si me enviara la factura||
p:le-escribo-para: Almost. You started with *usted*, so the verb takes *le* too.
I'm writing to is *para* in Spanish, never *a*.
te escribo para invitarle a almorzar||
*Te* means a friend, so the verb ends in *te* as well.
p:le-falta-sal: Almost. For what you taste right now, on this plate, Spanish prefers *está*.
Almost. The thing that lacks something needs *a* in front: *a la sopa*.
Almost. After *oler*, Spanish needs *a* before what you smell.
p:le-ruego-que: le ruego que me envía la factura||
Almost. After *ruego que* the verb needs the subjunctive, *envíe*.
le ruego para que me envíe la factura||
Almost. Spanish says *ruego que* with no *para*.
Almost. English says "ask you to send", but when someone else acts, Spanish needs *que* plus *envíe*.
p:llegar-a-inf: llegué para pensar que no volverías||
It is *a*, not *para*, and it is not about arriving anywhere.
The little *a* is needed before the infinitive.
After *a*, the second verb is an infinitive, not a gerund.
p:llegar-a-ser: Almost. English "became" is one word, but Spanish always puts *a* before *ser*.
Close. Without *ser*, *llegó a* just means she arrived somewhere.
llegué a ser nervioso antes de la entrevista||
*Llegar a ser* is for a long road, not for a quick change like getting nervous.
p:llegar-a-tiempo: English says "in time", but Spanish says *a tiempo*.
Almost. English says late *for*, but you arrive *a* somewhere: *tarde a la reunión*.
*Temprano* here is an adverb, so it stays the same for a woman.
p:lleno-libre: Almost. For is this seat taken, Spanish says *ocupado*.
Almost. Whether something is taken right now is a state, so *está*.
p:llevar-sin-inf: Almost. "Not" becomes *sin* here, and *no* is left out.
English says "without smoking", but after *sin* Spanish always uses the infinitive.
To count the time, use *llevar*, not *hacer* or *estar*.
p:llevar-tiempo-gerundio: estoy trabajando aquí por un año||
Almost. To say how long it's been going on, Spanish uses *llevar* plus the time.
*Trabajado* is the *he estado* ending; for how long, you need the *-ando* form.
After the time, the action takes the *-ando* or *-iendo* form, not the infinitive.
p:llevar-traer: llévame un vaso de agua por favor||
Almost. The water comes towards you, so it's *traer*.
The airport is away from here, so *llevar*, just as you'd say *ir*.
I bring is irregular: *traigo*, like *tengo* and *hago*.
p:lo-antes-posible: Almost. English "as soon as possible" is the fixed Spanish block *lo antes posible*.
vine lo más rápido que puedo||
Almost. For something that already happened, *poder* goes into the past: *pude*.
p:lo-de-noun: Almost. The "business about" is always *lo de*, never *la de*.
y el tuyo del trabajo qué tal||
For "your thing" in general, Spanish uses *lo tuyo*, not *el tuyo*.
You still need the *de*: *lo de ayer*.
p:lo-de-topic: la de la reunión me tiene preocupado||
Almost. It is not a feminine noun; *lo* is the neutral "matter", even before *la reunión*.
cómo va lo de el trabajo nuevo||
lo sobre la reunión me tiene preocupado||
Almost. Spanish links the matter with *de*, not with *sobre*.
p:lo-de: Almost. For a situation, use *lo*, never *el* or *la*.
lo de el contrato está listo||ya
English says *about*, but for news you both know of, Spanish points at it with *lo de*.
p:lo-mas-probable-es-que: lo más probable es que viene||
Almost. After *lo más probable es que*, Spanish uses the subjunctive, not the ordinary verb.
Keep the *de*: the frame is *probabilidades de que*.
lo más probable es se haya ido||ya
English drops "that" in "most likely he's left", but Spanish always keeps *que*.
p:lo-mas-recomendable: lo más recomendable es que consultas a un especialista||
Almost. After *lo más recomendable es que* the verb needs its subjunctive, *consultes*.
lo más recomendable es consultes a un especialista||
English can drop "that", but Spanish needs the *que* here.
le puedes que decir la verdad||siempre
After *siempre puedes* the verb is a plain infinitive, with no *que*.
p:lo-mejor-de: lo mejor la película es la fotografía||
Almost. You need *de* to say "about the film".
el mejor de la película es la fotografía||
Almost. "The best thing" has no noun, so Spanish uses *lo*, not *el*.
lo mejor de el café es el olor||
lo mejor de la película está la fotografía||
Almost. Naming what something is takes *es*.
p:lo-mejor-seria-que: lo mejor sería que vas al médico||
Almost. After *lo mejor sería que* Spanish wants the imagined verb, not the plain *vas*.
si sería hablaría con ella|tú yo|
Only the second half takes the *would* verb; after *si* use *fuera*.
te recomendaría que hablas con ella||
The verb after *que* takes the imagined form, *hablaras*, not *hablas*.
p:lo-mio-lo-tuyo: Almost. Spanish says "the yours" here: *lo tuyo* instead of "your thing".
*Lo* never changes, so the possessive stays *mío*.
The *lo* stays in front of the possessive.
p:lo-primero-que: la primera cosa que llama la atención es el silencio||
Almost. Spanish uses neuter *lo primero*, not "the first thing" word for word.
en primera vista parece un edificio normal||
visto desde afuera se parece abandonado||
p:lo-que-cosa-que: no llamó que me molestó bastante||
Almost. English "which" becomes *lo que* when it comments on the whole sentence.
no llamó el que me molestó bastante||
*El que* points at one masculine noun; for the whole situation you need *lo*.
p:lo-que-mas-me-gusta: lo que más me gusta es los domingos de ciclovía||
Almost. The verb agrees with what comes after it: plural, so *son*.
que más me gusta es el tráfico||
Almost. Spanish needs *lo* in front: *lo que*, "the thing that".
lo que más gusto es cocinar||
Almost. *Gustar* needs *me* to say who likes it: *me gusta*.
p:lo-que-pasa-es-que: lo que pasa que no tengo tiempo||
Almost. Don't drop the *es*: the block is *lo que pasa es que*.
qué pasa es que el carro no prende||
Almost. "What" here is *lo que*; *qué* alone asks a question.
lo que pasa es que no tengas tiempo||
Almost. You are stating a fact, so use the ordinary present: *tengo*.
p:lo-veo-dificil: Almost. English can drop the it, but Spanish needs the *lo* to point at the thing.
The *lo* goes in front of the verb. *Veo lo difícil* means I see the hard part.
When the thing is feminine, like *la audiencia*, the pointer is *la*.
p:los-celos-los-restos: tengo celos de tu carro nuevo||
Almost. *Celos* is about a person you fear losing. Wanting what someone has is *envidia*.
tiene un celo de su hermano||
Almost. In this meaning, *celos* never goes singular.
el resto del edificio estaban en la calle||
Almost. *El resto* is just "the rest"; the leftover pieces are *los restos*.
p:los-de-la-camiseta: me gusta más la una de la izquierda||
Almost. English needs "one"; Spanish needs nothing, just the article and *de*.
los de el segundo piso hacen mucho ruido||
Almost. After a number and *de*, you need the whole group: *mis*, *los*.
p:los-garcia: Almost. Spanish doesn't add an *s* to the surname; *los* already says it's the family.
*Los García* is several people, so the verb is plural: *viven*.
The name comes after *familia*, not before it.
p:lugar-tiene: Almost. *Hay* can't take the place as its subject: either the place *tiene* it, or you say *En mi barrio hay un parque*.
After *en* and the place, nobody is doing the having, so the verb is *hay*.
*Tener* matches the place doing the having: one room *tiene*, two rooms *tienen*.
p:madrugar-trasnochar: Almost. The person goes in the little word *me*, and the verb is *toca*.
*Madrugar* is getting up early, not arriving early. For arriving early, use *llegar temprano*.
No little word goes between *toca* and the infinitive.
p:mancharse: Close. When it lands on you, use *me* and *la*, not *mi*.
Almost. The thing that gets dirty comes after the verb, and the stuff comes after *de*.
Without *me*, it sounds like you stained some shirt, not the one you had on.
p:mas-de-lo-que: Almost. Before a verb Spanish needs *de lo que*, not just *que*.
hay más gente de lo que pensaba||
When a noun is compared, the article matches it: *gente* takes *la*.
Plural masculine noun, so *de los que*.
p:mas-de-number: Almost. Before a number, Spanish uses *de*, not *que*.
With a person to compare with, it's *que*; *de* is only for numbers.
*Menos* follows the same rule: before a number, *menos de*.
p:masculine-plural-mixed: pablo y ana son mis hermanas||
Almost. Pablo is a man, so the group is *hermanos*; *hermanas* means sisters only.
*Parientes* means relatives. Your parents are *mis papás*.
The describing word follows the group: several people, so *simpáticos*.
p:mayor-menor: Almost. *Mayor* and *menor* go after the noun, like colours.
*Vieja* means old, as in elderly, and she won't thank you. Siblings are *mayor* or *menor*.
*Mayor* ends in a consonant, so the plural adds *es*: *mayores*.
p:me-aburre-que: aburro que hablen de lo mismo|yo|
Almost. The talking bores you, so the verb agrees with it (*aburre*) and you are *me*.
me aburre que hablan de lo mismo||siempre
Almost. After *me aburre que*, the verb takes its "other" ending, so *hablan* becomes *hablen*.
Almost. Without *de*, the waiting is what bores you, so use *aburre*. If you are the one getting bored, add *de*: *Me aburro de esperar*.
p:me-aburre: Almost. With *yo aburro* you are the one boring the meetings; let the meetings do it to you.
The meetings do the boring, so the verb is plural.
me cansa de manejar de noche||
The infinitive follows directly, with no *de*.
p:me-comunica-con: me comunica a la señora gómez||
Almost. Connecting someone is always *comunicar con*, never *a*.
me conecta con la señora gómez||
Almost. On the phone, Spanish uses *comunicar*; *conectar* is for cables and the internet.
Almost. On a call to people you don't know, use *usted*: *comunica*, not *comunicas*.
p:me-contaron-que: me han contado que te vas para españa||
Almost. In Latin America the simple past is the everyday choice.
me contaron te vas para españa||
Almost. Spanish needs *que* before the news, even when English drops "that".
dicen de que hay novio nuevo||
p:me-da-miedo-que: Almost. Spanish keeps the *de* before *que*, where English drops *of*.
The verb agrees with the thing that scares you, and heights are plural.
me da miedo que manejas tan rápido||
After *que*, a feeling about someone else's action wants the subjunctive.
p:me-da-miedo: Close. An action counts as one thing, so *da*.
me da miedo de los perros||
With *me da miedo*, the thing comes straight after with no *de*, and several dogs take *dan*.
*Yo* doesn't fit this shape, because you aren't doing the verb. For weight on *me*, say *A mí me da miedo*.
p:me-da-pena-que: me da pena que estás solo||
Almost. After a feeling about someone else, use the subjunctive: *estés*.
tengo pena que no puedas venir||
Spanish doesn't "have" the sadness. It's given to you: *me da pena*.
me da pena que hablar delante de todos||
Almost. When you're the one acting, drop *que* and use the infinitive.
p:me-da-rabia-me-indigna: me da rabia de que no me hayas avisado||
Almost. Spanish has no *de* before *que* here.
Almost. After *no aguanto que* the verb takes the subjunctive: *interrumpan*.
me da rabia que no me avisaste||
Almost. For something already done, use *hayas* plus the *-ado* form.
p:me-da-rabia-que: me da rabia que me interrumpen||
Almost. After *me da rabia que*, the verb takes the subjunctive: *interrumpan*.
me da rabia que perder el bus||
Almost. When you're the one acting, drop *que* and use the infinitive.
tengo rabia que altamira compre todo||
Almost. *Tengo rabia* works on its own, but before *que* Spanish says the event gives you the anger: *me da rabia que*.
p:me-da-verguenza: Careful. *Embarazada* means pregnant. For embarrassed, let the shame *give* itself to you.
Almost. *Yo doy vergüenza* means you embarrass other people. When you feel it, it's *me da*.
me da vergüenza que me ven así||
Almost. After *que*, the verb takes the subjunctive: *vean*.
p:me-decepciono-que: me dolió que no me invitaron||
Almost. After *que* in a feeling, use the subjunctive: *invitaran*.
The thing that let you down is the subject: *me decepcionó*.
Use *con* for what let you down.
English makes you the subject; Spanish puts *me* in front, like *gustar*.
p:me-duele-que: me duele que no te puedo ayudar||
Almost. When it's your own inability, there's no *que*: use the infinitive.
duelo que altamira diga eso de rosa|yo|
The event is what hurts, so you become *me* and the verb is *duele*.
me duele que altamira dice eso de rosa||
Almost. After *me duele que*, the verb takes the subjunctive: *diga*.
p:me-duele: Almost. *Me* already says whose head it is, so it's *la cabeza*.
Two feet, so *duelen*. The verb follows the body part, not you.
English starts with *my back*. Spanish starts with *me duele* and puts the body part after.
p:me-emociona-que: Almost. The news excites you, so *me* comes first and the verb stays *emociona*.
A feeling about someone else's action wants the subjunctive: *vengas*.
No little word is needed before the infinitive.
p:me-encanta-que: Almost. After *me gusta que* the verb takes the subjunctive, *llamen*.
Almost. If you are the one cooking, use the infinitive, no *que*.
Almost. A noun needs no *que*; keep *que* for a clause with its own verb.
p:me-extrana-que: me extraña que no ha llamado||
Almost. A reaction to a fact still takes the subjunctive, so *ha* becomes *haya*.
Almost. English keeps "you're", but Spanish switches to *estés*.
Almost. *Extraño* alone means "I miss"; to be surprised you need *me extraña*.
p:me-hace-el-favor: me haces un favor de cerrar la ventana||
Almost. This polite formula always uses *el favor*, not *un favor*.
me hace el favor y pasarme la sal||
After *y* Spanish wants a regular conjugated verb, not an infinitive.
me haces el favor y me pasa la sal||
Keep one way of addressing the person: *haces* goes with *pasas*, *hace* with *pasa*.
p:me-haces-el-favor-de: me haces el favor de cerrando la puerta||
Almost. English says "of closing", but after *de* Spanish wants the dictionary form, *cerrar*.
me haces un favor de cerrar la puerta||
Almost. With *de* and a verb, the set phrase is *el favor*, not *un favor*.
me haces el favor de esperar un momento||
Almost. With someone you call *usted*, the verb is *hace*, not *haces*.
p:me-harias-un-favor: Almost. The phrase is *hacer un favor*, and Spanish needs the *un*.
necesitaría que me cuidas a los niños||
Almost. After *necesitaría que* use the *-ra* form, not the plain present.
necesito que alguien me ayuda con las cajas||
Almost. *Necesito que* needs the subjunctive: *ayude*, not *ayuda*.
p:me-hubieras-dicho: Almost. A reproach about what did not happen needs *hubieras* + *dicho*.
me habías dicho y te ayudaba||
English "had told" pulls you to *habías dicho*, but that says you really did tell me. The reproach needs *hubieras*.
p:me-parece-bien-que: Almost. After *me parece bien que*, use the subjunctive: *vengas*.
me parece mal altamira compre la cuadra||
When someone else does it, Spanish needs *que* before the new subject.
Don't forget *me*: it says who is judging.
p:me-parecio-mal-que: me pareció mal que te fuiste||
Almost. After a judgement like this, Spanish uses the *-ra* form, not the plain past.
me pareció mal de que te fueras||
me pareció mal que te vas||
Almost. After *me pareció mal que*, the verb takes the *-ra* form.
p:me-permito: me permito a informarle que su solicitud fue aprobada||
permito informarle que su solicitud fue aprobada||
Without *me* it means "I allow", which is not the polite formula.
me permito informarte que su solicitud fue aprobada||
*Me permito* is formal, so it goes with *le* (*usted*), not *te*.
p:me-pone-de-buen-genio: la lluvia me hace de mal genio||
Almost. For "puts me in a mood" Spanish uses *poner*, not *hacer*.
la lluvia me pone en mal genio||
Almost. English says "in a mood", but Spanish says *de* here.
madrugar me pone de malo genio||
Almost. *Malo* loses its *-o* in front of a masculine noun: *mal genio*.
p:me-pone-nervioso-que: me pone nerviosa que no contestas los mensajes||
Almost. After a feeling plus *que*, the verb takes the subjunctive: *contestes*.
yo desespero la lentitud de este trámite||
Almost. The slowness is what does the driving crazy, and you are the *me*.
Almost. Spanish says *la paciencia* here, not *mi paciencia*.
p:me-pone-nervioso: English says *makes*, but Spanish puts you in a mood with *poner*, not *hacer*.
*Me pongo* means you change by yourself; when something causes it, the cause is the subject: *pone*.
The verb agrees with the cause (*las reuniones*, plural), while the adjective agrees with you.
p:me-pongo-triste-cuando: soy triste cuando oigo esa canción||
Almost. *Ser* describes who you are; a reaction that comes and goes is *ponerse*.
*Me pongo* is for a change that happens; how you feel at this moment is *estoy*.
nos ponemos triste cuando se va||
The feeling word agrees with *we*, so it becomes plural.
p:me-preocupa-que: Almost. The little word after *preocupado* is *por*, never *de*.
The ending *-ísimo* already means extremely, so *muy* is one too many.
The news worries you, so *me* comes first and the verb stays *preocupa*.
p:me-sorprende-me-sorprendo: Almost. Without *me*, you are the one doing the surprising; for "it surprises me" the *me* has to come first.
me sorprende de que esté vacía||
Almost. With *me sorprende* there is no *de*; *me sorprendo de que* has it.
Almost. The verb agrees with what causes the feeling, and *sus preguntas* is plural.
p:me-sorprende-que: After a feeling about someone's action, the verb goes into the subjunctive.
Almost. Without *me*, *extraño* means *I miss*; the surprised meaning needs *me extraña*.
estoy sorprendido que vale no esté aquí||
English says *I'm surprised*; Spanish turns it round, so the fact does the surprising: *me sorprende*.
p:me-te-nos-objects: Almost. In Spanish, *me* goes in front of the verb.
*No* comes first, then *te*: nothing goes between *te* and the verb.
*Yo* is the person doing it. For 'me' on the receiving end, use *me* before the verb.
p:me-temo-que: tengo miedo que no va a poder ser||
Almost. For "I'm afraid" in the polite sense, Spanish uses *me temo que*.
me temo que no tengamos mesa||
Almost. Here *temerse* reports bad news as a fact, so the verb stays ordinary.
me temo no va a poder ser||
Almost. The bad news after "I'm afraid" always needs *que*.
p:me-trae: Almost. In a question like this, *me* goes in front of the verb.
*Otra* already means 'another', so it never takes *una*.
A bare order sounds bossy to a waiter. Ask it as a question, in the *usted* form.
p:medir-pesar-caber: Almost. Size isn't said with *ser*; Spanish uses *medir*.
el sofá no cabe la puerta||
*Caber* needs a small word before the place: *por* for passing through, *en* for being inside.
p:medir-pesar: Almost. In Spanish you don't *are* a height, you measure it: *mido*.
*How tall* doesn't carry over word for word. Ask how much: *¿Cuánto mides?*
Like *pedir*, the e turns into i: *mido*.
p:medir: Almost. Spanish doesn't use *ser* for size: the table measures two metres.
Seventy metres on its own is a length. For area, say *cuadrados*.
The vowel changes in *mido*, *mides*, *mide* and *miden*, like *pido*.
p:miedo-a: Almost. English says *I am afraid*, but in Spanish you *have* fear: *tengo miedo*.
After *a*, a verb stays as an infinitive, not *-ando*.
With *me da miedo*, the verb comes straight after, with no *a*.
p:mientras-subj: Almost. After *mientras* meaning "as long as", Spanish uses the present subjunctive, never the future.
With the indicative it would just mean "while there is work"; to set a condition you need *haya*.
To say "as long as it doesn't rain", use *no llueva*. The indicative *llueve* would mean "while it is raining".
p:mira-que: Almost. You are stating a fact, so the verb stays ordinary: *eres*.
Almost. *Mire* speaks to *usted*, so the verb must be *es*.
p:mirar-por-encima-del-hombro: miró a mí por encima del hombro||
Almost. The person looked down on is a small word before the verb: *me*, *la*, *nos*.
Almost. The look goes both ways: *de arriba abajo*.
Almost. The fixed phrase is *por encima del hombro*, with no swaps.
p:morirse-de: Almost. Spanish says it with the small word: *me muero*, or *me estoy muriendo*.
Almost. The feeling you die of comes after *de*, not *por*.
Almost. "Dying to" needs *ganas*: *de ganas de* plus an infinitive.
p:naci-en: Almost. Spanish doesn't say was born with two words; it's just *nací*.
Close. A full date takes *el* alone; *en* is for a year or a place.
Nearly. Born in a place is *en*, never *a*.
p:negar-confesar: Almost. After *negar que*, the verb takes the *-ra* form.
Almost. Confessing accepts the fact, so an ordinary verb follows, not the *-ra* form.
el funcionario negó a saber la respuesta||
Almost. *Negar* goes straight into the infinitive, with no *a*.
p:news-quantities: Almost. When something grows by itself, Spanish adds *se*: *se duplicó*.
un tercio de estudiantes no votó||
Spanish keeps the article after *de*: *de los estudiantes*.
el precio se redujo la mitad||
You need the *a*: *se redujo a la mitad*.
p:ni-aunque: no vuelvo ni aunque me pagan||
Almost. A possible offer after *ni aunque* takes the subjunctive.
ni aunque me pagaran el doble vuelvo||
Almost. After an imaginary offer, the refusal is in the conditional.
Almost. *Aunque* needs a conjugated verb, not the infinitive.
p:ni-emphatic: Almost. For a flat "no way", *ni* does the work, not *no*.
Almost. After *ni*, the sentence stays negative, so you need *nadie*, not *alguien*.
Almost. On its own, Colombian *siquiera* means *good thing*: *¡Siquiera me saludó!* is relief. For *not even*, say *ni siquiera*.
p:ninguna-parte: veo mi celular en ninguna parte||
Almost. Spanish needs the *no* before the verb as well.
no lo encuentro por ninguna lado||
p:no-crees-que: no crees que sea muy caro||
Almost. In this question you believe it is expensive, so the verb stays in the indicative.
no creo que es muy caro||
A plain *no creo que* is doubt, and doubt takes the subjunctive.
With a friend you say *crees*; *cree* is for *usted*.
p:no-deberias-haberlo-hecho: Almost. When the pronoun goes after *haber*, it joins it as one word.
Only *deberías* changes for the person; *haber* stays as it is.
p:no-digo-que-pero: no digo que está mal pero no lo haría|yo|
Almost. English says "I'm not saying it is", but Spanish needs the subjunctive after *no digo que*.
no digo que esté mal pero no lo haga|yo|
Almost. Only the half after *que* is subjunctive; the *pero* half is your real statement.
digo que no sea mala pero es muy larga|yo|
Almost. The *no* goes before *digo*: you are refusing to say it, not saying the opposite.
p:no-dude-en: no dude llamarme si tiene alguna pregunta||
no duda en llamarme si tiene alguna pregunta||
Almost. A polite negative command uses the subjunctive: *dude*, not *duda*.
estoy a su disposición por cualquier consulta||
Almost. What you are available for takes *para*.
p:no-es-nada-adj: Close. Before an adjective, *demasiado* never changes. Only *caras* agrees.
Careful. *Demasiado* usually means too much, so this can sound like a problem. For praise, *muy* is the safe choice. You'll still hear people use *demasiado* as praise: *está demasiado rico*.
English puts *at all* at the end. Spanish puts *nada* right before the adjective.
p:no-es-que-sino-que: no es que es caro sino que no lo necesito||
Almost. The idea you are rejecting after *no es que* takes the subjunctive: *sea*.
no es que no quiera ir es que tenga que trabajar||
Almost. The real reason is a fact, so the verb stays ordinary: *tengo*.
no es que sea caro sino no lo necesito||
Almost. Before a full clause, *sino* needs *que*.
p:no-es-x-es-y: To *No hablas español, ¿no?*, English says yes, I do. Spanish repeats the real verb: *sí hablo*.
no es no de cali es de medellín||
Almost. *No* always goes before the verb: *no es*, never *es no*.
p:no-estar-para: Almost. This is a state you are in today, so Spanish uses *estar*, not *ser*.
no estoy en el humor para bromas||
Almost. Spanish skips "in the mood": *no estoy para* already says it.
p:no-estoy-seguro-de-que: no estoy seguro de que viene||
Almost. When you doubt, the verb after *de que* takes the subjunctive.
Almost. English drops *of*, but Spanish needs *de* before *que*.
Almost. When you're certain, the verb stays ordinary.
p:no-hace-falta-que: no hace falta que traes nada||
Almost. After *que* here the verb needs its subjunctive, *traigas*.
Almost. *No debes* sounds like a ban; *no hace falta* just lifts the duty.
no tienes por qué que te disculpes||
Almost. *No tienes por qué* takes a plain infinitive, with no *que*.
p:no-hasta: la abogada llega hasta el lunes||
Without *no*, *hasta* means until, as if she were here until Monday. For not until, keep the *no*.
*Hasta que* is for a clause with a verb. A plain time takes just *hasta*.
no me voy hasta que llegas||
It hasn't happened yet, so *hasta que* takes the subjunctive: *llegues*.
p:no-me-cabe-duda: no me cabe duda de que vale tenga razón||
Almost. You have no doubt, so the verb stays ordinary; the subjunctive is for when you do doubt.
no me cabe duda que vale tiene razón||
Almost. After *duda* Spanish keeps the *de* in front of *que*.
consto que hernando pagó la cuenta|yo|
Almost. The fact is what is "clear" to you, so you are *me*, like in *me gusta*.
p:no-me-extrana-que: no me extraña que estás tan disgustado||
Almost. After *no me extraña que* the verb is in the subjunctive: *estés*.
simpatizo con lo que estás pasando||
Almost. *Simpatizar* means to like someone; to show you feel for them, say *me imagino lo que...*
p:no-me-olvido-de: no he olvidado de tu cumpleaños||
Almost. With *de*, the verb is *olvidarse*, so it needs its *me*.
nunca olvidaré de cómo nos ayudaron||
*Olvidar* without the *me* takes the thing directly, with no *de*.
no me he olvidado tu cumpleaños||
English "forget" takes nothing in between, but once the *me* is there, Spanish needs the *de*.
p:no-porque-sino-porque: no estudia porque tiene miedo sino porque le interesa||
Almost. The reason you reject takes the "maybe" form: *tenga*.
no lo digo porque sea mi amigo sino porque sea verdad||
Almost. The real reason is a fact, so it stays ordinary: *es*.
no lo digo porque sea mi amigo pero porque es verdad||
Almost. After a "not this", the "but rather" is *sino*, not *pero*.
p:no-queda-de-otra: no hay más remedio de esperar||
Almost. The frame closes with *que*, not *de*.
Almost. *Toca* is followed straight by the infinitive, with no *que*.
no hay más remedio que esperamos||
Almost. Nobody is named in this frame, so the verb stays as a plain infinitive.
p:no-quedar-mas-remedio: no me quedó más remedio de cancelar||
Almost. The link to the infinitive is *que*, not *de*.
no nos quedaron más remedio que cancelar||
Almost. *Remedio* is singular, so the verb is *quedó*.
nos no quedó más remedio que cancelar||
Almost. *No* comes first, then the pronoun: *no nos quedó*.
p:no-recuerdo-que-subj: Almost. When you are not vouching for it, the verb after *que* takes the *-ra* form.
no me acuerdo que me lo prometieras||
no recuerdo a vale llamando esa noche||
Almost. English says "Vale calling", but Spanish uses *que* and a full verb.
p:no-se-que-hacer: Close. English needs to, but Spanish doesn't: *hacer* already means to do, so no *para*.
Whether is *si* with no accent. *Sí* means yes.
p:no-servir-para-nada: Almost. English "no use at all" hides the little word; Spanish needs *para*.
esos aparatos no sirve para nada||
Almost. The verb agrees with the thing, and there are several.
Almost. *Estorbo* is masculine, even when the table is feminine.
p:no-soportar-que: Almost. After *no soporto que*, the verb takes the subjunctive: *interrumpan*.
*Stand* here has nothing to do with standing up. Spanish uses *soportar*: *no soporto*.
Almost. When you're the one acting, drop *que* and use the infinitive.
p:no-soporto-que: Almost. After *no soporto que*, the verb takes its "other" ending, so *-ar* verbs switch to *-en*.
Almost. When you are the one doing both verbs, Spanish uses the infinitive and drops *que*.
no lo soporto que me interrumpan||
Almost. English needs "it", Spanish doesn't: the *que* part is already the thing you can't stand.
p:no-te-falta-razon: no tienes razón bien hay que pensar en el costo||ahora
Careful. *No tienes razón* means "you're wrong"; to grant a point, use *no te falta razón*.
Spanish drops the article here, as in *tienes razón*.
p:no-te-imaginas-lo-que: Almost. English says "how tired", but Spanish swaps *cómo* for *lo* and adds *que*: *lo cansado que*.
no te imagina lo que me pasó don hernando||
With *usted*, the pronoun changes too: *se imagina*, not *te imagina*.
no te imaginas lo que pasó me||
The *me* goes before the verb: *me pasó*.
p:no-tener-ni-idea-de: The little word *de* links the idea to what comes after.
tengo ni idea de qué hacer||
Spanish needs *no* before the verb as well as *ni*: two negatives, one meaning.
no tenía ni idea que estabas aquí||
p:no-tengas-miedo-de: Almost. *Tienes* only states a fact; to encourage someone, use *tengas*.
Making a mistake is *equivocarse*, so it keeps its little word: *equivocarte*.
*Atreverse* always needs *a* before the next verb.
p:no-tengo-tan-claro: no tengo tan claro que es la mejor solución||
Almost. You are doubting, so the verb after *que* takes the subjunctive.
pongo en duda de que el senador diga la verdad||
Almost. *Poner en duda* takes *que* directly, with no *de*.
tengo claro que altamira tenga el permiso||
Almost. Without *no* you are sure, so the verb stays ordinary.
p:no-vayas-a: no vas a perder las llaves||
Almost. *No vas a* says you won't; to warn someone, use *vayas*.
The little *a* stays before the infinitive.
When something happens to you, like a fall, add *te*.
p:nos-vemos-a-las: Days take *el*, not *en*: *el viernes* means 'on Friday'.
Clock times take *a*: *a las siete*, never *en*.
One is singular, so *a la una*.
p:nosotros-instructions: Almost. "Sit down" is *sentarse*, so the *we* form needs *nos*.
nos prendemos la máquina y nos esperamos unos minutos||
Almost. *Nos* is only for things we do to ourselves, not for a machine or for waiting.
p:numbers-un-una: No *y* after the hundred. *Y* only joins tens and ones: *treinta y uno*.
A thousand is just *mil*, with no *un*.
p:o-sea-que: Almost. Join it with *que*, or put a comma after *o sea*.
no es tímido o sea que es reservado||
Almost. *O sea que* draws a conclusion; to swap a word for a better one, use *mejor dicho*.
hay 3 ofertas mejor dicho hay 3 ofertas||
*Mejor dicho* has to bring a new version, or there is nothing to correct.
p:obligacion-origen: Almost. Being obliged is a state you are in, so it takes *estar*.
Almost. *Obligar* always needs *a* before the next verb.
Almost. *Obligación* is followed directly by the verb, with no *a*.
p:ocurrir-producirse: Almost. The verb agrees with the event, and one fire is singular.
Almost. The accidents are plural, so the verb is too: *ocurrieron*.
el accidente ocurrió a la madrugada||
Almost. "In the early hours" is *de madrugada* (or *en la madrugada*).
p:ocurrirsele: Almost. The idea is what happens; you are the one it happens to.
The verb agrees with the ideas, not with you.
Without *se*, *ocurrir* just means "to happen". Keep the *se*.
p:oir-hablar-de: has oído hablar que cerraron la calle||
Almost. *Hablar de* goes with a thing; a whole piece of news takes *oí que* or *supiste que*.
oí hablar que altamira compró el edificio||
Drop *hablar*: for news you just need *oí que*.
English says *heard of*; Spanish keeps the little word *de*.
p:ojala-hubiera: After *hubiera* you need the participle (*tenido*), not the infinitive.
*Tuviera* is a wish about now. For yesterday, say *hubiera tenido*.
p:ojo-con-no-confies: Almost. The warning word is always followed by *con*.
As an order to a friend, the verb takes *-es*; *confías* would only state a fact.
p:oler-a-saber-a: Almost. To say what it smells of, Spanish needs the small word *a*.
A substance takes no article, so just *a ajo*.
p:orden-sin-imperativo: Almost. *Quedarse* in the sense of staying needs *te*.
Almost. After *lo que* the verb is *diga*, not *dices*.
Almost. To say "you" the verb ends in *-ás*, not *-á*.
p:ordinal-floor: Almost. *Cuatro* is the count; for the fourth one, Spanish says *cuarto*.
Right before a masculine word, *primero* drops its *o*: *el primer día*.
Only the masculine shortens. With a feminine word it stays *primera*.
p:ordinals-primer-tercer: Almost. Right before a masculine noun, *primero* drops its *o*: *primer día*.
*Vez* is feminine, and the shortening only happens before masculine words.
p:orgulloso-admiracion: Almost. English says "proud of", and Spanish matches it with *de*.
Almost. English says "What a view", but Spanish drops the *una*.
estoy muy orgulloso de que has venido||
Almost. A feeling about a fact takes the subjunctive: *hayas venido*.
p:otro-no-article: Almost. *otro* already has the "an" inside it, so drop the *un*.
*arepa* is a *la* word, so it takes *otra*.
Two more is *otros dos*: the number comes after *otros*.
p:para-inf-purpose: estudio español para quiero vivir aquí||
Almost. *Para* takes the basic verb directly; a conjugated verb like *quiero* goes after *porque*.
uso esta aplicación para mando audios||
After *para*, the verb keeps its dictionary form: *mandar*.
English says just to send; Spanish needs *para* in front.
p:para-inf: After *para*, the verb keeps its -ar ending: *trabajar*, not *trabajo*.
vale llega a las 5 hacer el pan||
English can say just "to make", but Spanish needs *para* in front.
estudio español por trabajar en bogotá||
For a goal, Spanish uses *para*. *Por* is a different word you'll meet later.
p:para-mi-que: para yo que no sabe nada||
por mí que aquí pasa algo raro||
Almost. The hunch opener is *para mí*; *por mí* means "as far as I'm concerned" in a different way.
Almost. It is a hunch you believe, so the verb stays ordinary: *es*.
p:para-mi: para yo el ajiaco es delicioso||
para mi el ajiaco es delicioso||
Without the accent, *mi* means my; you need *mí*.
p:para-que-rhetorical: por qué me esfuerzo si nadie lo nota||
Almost. *Por qué* asks for the cause; *para qué* asks about the point, which is what "why bother" means.
para qué esfuerzo si nadie lo nota||
para qué cocino tanto para ganar plata||
Almost. As a complaint, it is not answered; add the *si* part that says why it is pointless.
p:para-ser: por ser tan joven sabe mucho||
Almost. *Por* would mean "because she's so young", which makes no sense here; "for someone so young" takes *para*.
habla muy bien para tener un año aquí||
For a length of time, Spanish says *llevar*: *llevar un año aquí*.
no está mal por la primera vez||
p:para-terminar: en corto el café es de todos||
Almost. "In short" is not *en corto*; Spanish says *en resumen*.
To an audience, use the formal *su*, not *tu*.
en resumen además el café es de todos||
A closing line adds nothing new, so *además* has no place there.
p:parece-mentira-que: parece mentira que pasó un año||ya
Almost. A reaction takes the subjunctive, and for something finished that is *haya pasado*.
parece mentira de que sea tan tarde||
Almost. There is no *de* before *que* here.
parece que mentira que sea tan tarde||
Almost. *Parece mentira* stays together, and *que* comes after.
p:parecer-vs-parecerse: Almost. To look like a person you need *se parece a*.
For how someone seems, drop the *se*.
p:parecerse-a: Almost. *Mirar* is to look at something. To look like someone, Spanish says *parecerse a*.
The I form has a k sound in it: *parezco*, like *conozco*.
p:pasar-hambre-frio: Almost. For hunger you feel right now, Spanish uses *tener*.
Almost. The tiring thing is the subject, and it is plural, so the verb is too.
esa noche estuvimos muy fríos en el páramo||
Almost. English says "we were cold", but in Spanish people don't *be* cold: you have it (*tener frío*) or go through it (*pasar frío*).
p:pasar-por-alto: pasó por el alto el error||
Almost. The phrase is fixed: *por alto*, with no *el* in the middle.
Almost. Spanish needs *le* in front and *a* before the thing played down.
pasamos por alto a la pregunta||
Almost. *Pasar por alto* takes the thing directly; the little *a* only goes before a person.
p:pasarla-bien-mal: Almost. Without *la* it sounds like you walked past something.
*Lo pasé* is what people say in Spain; in Latin America it's *la pasé*.
tuve un buen tiempo en la fiesta||
English says *I had a good time*, but *tener un buen tiempo* isn't Spanish for it. Say *la pasé bien*.
p:pasarla-bien: tuve un buen tiempo en la fiesta||
Had a good time doesn't translate word for word; Spanish says *la pasé bien*.
Almost. The phrase always keeps its *la*.
The *la* never changes, even when it's a group.
p:pasarse-la-vida: se pasa la vida a quejarse||
Almost. After *pasarse* the activity is the *-ando* or *-iendo* form: no *a*, no infinitive.
Almost. Yesterday is over, so *pasé*, not *paso*.
Almost. It is *we* doing it, so the verb is *pasamos*.
p:pase-lo-que-pase: pasa lo que pasa te apoyo||
Almost. Plain *pasa* describes what actually happens; the 'whatever' feeling needs the subjunctive, *pase*.
pase lo que ocurra te apoyo||
Say the same verb twice; swapping in a synonym breaks the pattern.
English starts with "whatever", but Spanish needs the verb first and again at the end: *pase lo que pase*.
p:pedir-disculpas-por: le pido disculpas para la demora||
Almost. The reason for an apology comes with *por*, never *para*.
te pido disculpas de llegar tarde||
Close. English says "sorry for", and Spanish says *por*.
disculpe es que no te vi||
Stay in one register: *disculpe* is for *usted*, so the person is *lo* or *la*, not *te*.
p:pensaba-pero: me pensé quedar en casa pero salí||
Almost. The simple past sounds like a decision you made and carried out; a plan that stayed unfinished uses the imperfect.
te voy a llamar pero no tuve tiempo||
The plan happened in the past too, so *ir* goes in the imperfect.
te iba llamar pero no tuve tiempo||
*Ir* needs its *a* before the next verb.
p:pensar-en: Almost. *Pensar de* only shows up in *¿Qué piensas de...?*, which asks an opinion.
pienso en que es un error||
Almost. For an opinion there is no *en*: *pienso que* plus the sentence.
p:pensar-inf: Almost. *Pienso* goes straight to the verb, with no *a* or *de* in between.
estoy pensando de viajar en diciembre||
English says thinking of, but Spanish says *pensando en*.
After *pienso*, English could use -ing, but Spanish wants the dictionary form: *ir*.
p:perdona-que-interrumpa: perdona que te interrumpo pero es tarde||ya
After *perdona que*, the verb ends in *-a*: *interrumpa*, not *interrumpo*.
disculpe que te interrumpa pero es urgente||
Almost. With *usted*, the pronoun is *lo* or *la*, not *te*.
lo siento para interrumpir pero es tarde||ya
English *sorry to* doesn't carry over word for word. Spanish says *perdona que te interrumpa*.
p:perdona-que-te-interrumpa: Almost. After *perdona que*, Spanish needs the subjunctive, *interrumpa*, not the usual present.
perdone que te interrumpa pero es importante||
*Perdone* is formal, so the pronoun must match: *lo* or *la*, not *te*.
perdona interrumpirte pero es hora de irnos||ya
English "sorry to interrupt" uses an infinitive. Spanish says *perdona que te interrumpa*, or *perdón por interrumpirte*.
p:perfecto-still-live: Almost. Yesterday is finished, and in Latin America a finished day takes the simple past.
he pensado que ha sido un error||siempre
Only the view is still alive. The mistake itself is a closed event, so it takes *fue*.
nunca he entendido por qué ha renunciado||
The resignation happened once and is over, so keep it in the simple past.
p:permitir-inf: Almost. Spanish puts the infinitive right after the verb, with no *a* in between.
The person goes in the little word before the verb: *le*.
el médico me prohibió de fumar||
English says "banned from smoking", but Spanish puts the infinitive straight after the verb, with no *de*.
p:personal-a: Almost. Vale is a person, so Spanish wants *a* in front.
*Tener* is the exception: no *a*, even for people.
Cities and things don't get the *a*; only people do.
p:personalmente-tecnicamente: Almost. *Personal* is an adjective; to frame a whole sentence you need the adverb with *-mente*.
Almost. To frame the claim, put the adverb first, with a comma.
p:pesar-pesarse: Almost. Spanish does not use *ser* for weight; the thing *weighs* an amount.
Use *me* only when you weigh yourself. For a suitcase, say *peso la maleta*.
Nothing is weighing itself here, so there is no *se*.
p:plata-no-hay: Almost. A bare noun in front takes no pronoun, so no *la*.
Almost. For "any money" at all, drop the article.
Almost. The *no* stays right before the verb.
p:plazos: Almost. Spanish marks these distances with *a*, not *en*.
a la largo es más barato||
Almost. After *la*, the word is *larga*, the feminine form.
a medio plazo vamos a cambiar||
Almost. *Medio plazo* is the Spain version; in Latin America you will hear *mediano plazo*.
p:plural-one-object: Almost. *Pantalones* is plural, so the article must be too.
Almost. Scissors are plural in Spanish, just like in English.
Almost. *Virus* has no separate plural ending; the article shows it.
p:poco-un-poco: Almost. *De* only comes before a thing, like *un poco de agua*. Before a describing word, just *un poco*.
*Un poco* never changes, even before a feminine word like *agua*.
Before a thing, *un poco* needs *de*: *un poco de agua*.
p:podria-hablar-con: Almost. On the phone you speak *con* a person, not *a*.
It is understood, but *quería* is much more polite.
When answering, *¿De parte de quién?* is the polite way to ask who is calling.
p:podriamos-deberiamos: podríamos a ir a la montaña||
Almost. These verbs go straight into the infinitive, with no *a* and no *que*.
Almost. Only *tenemos que* has *que*; *deberíamos* does not.
Almost. "We have to" needs *que* before the infinitive.
p:podrias-haber: The pronoun joins *haber* in one word, or goes before *podrías*: *me podrías haber avisado*.
After *haber* the participle always ends in *-ado* or *-ido*.
Without *haber* the sentence is incomplete; "could have" needs all three pieces.
p:ponerse-a-inf: Almost. *Ponerse* always takes *a* before the next verb.
no me quiero poner a llorando||
English says start crying, but after *a* Spanish wants the dictionary form: *llorar*.
hernando me va a poner a cantar||
The little word follows the person: for Hernando it's *ponerse*.
me voy a poner a la chaqueta||
With clothes there's no *a*: *ponerse la chaqueta* is just put on.
p:ponerse-a: You need the *a* before the second verb.
Almost. With a feeling there is no *a*: *ponerse triste* is a change of mood.
Without *se*, *poner* means to place something somewhere; the starting meaning needs *se*.
p:ponerse-al-tanto: estoy en el tanto de la situación||
Almost. The phrase is *al tanto*, one block.
Almost. You need *de* before the topic.
p:ponerse-en-el-lugar: Almost. Without *te* you are asking someone to put something there; you want them to put themselves.
Spanish uses place, not shoes; *zapatos* would only mean footwear.
me puse en el lugar a vale||
The place belongs to Vale, so the link is *de*, not *a*.
p:por-casualidad: en casualidad sabe dónde queda la notaría||
Almost. The phrase is fixed: it is always *por casualidad*.
nos encontramos por accidente en el aeropuerto||
*Por accidente* is for mishaps, like breaking something. A lucky meeting is *por casualidad*.
por la casualidad sabe dónde queda la notaría||
No article: the phrase is just *por casualidad*.
p:por-ciento: Almost. English says "by", but Spanish uses *un*, not *por*.
el 30 por 100 clientes compra por internet||
Almost. After the figure you need *de* before the group.
p:por-cierto-hablando-de: Almost. *Hablando de* needs the thing you are linking to right after it.
hablando de simón no hay clase||mañana
*Hablando de* promises a link. If the new thought has none, use *por cierto*.
por la manera no hay clase||mañana
English "by the way" doesn't translate word for word. Spanish says *por cierto*.
p:por-consenso: Almost. The way a decision was reached is always *por*.
Almost. The frame has no article, just like English "by consensus".
la junta hizo el visto bueno||
Almost. Approval is something you give, so the verb is *dar*.
p:por-culpa-de: Almost. For yourself, Spanish uses *mía*, not *de mí*.
Close. For your friend it is *tuya*, a single word.
por culpa de ella todo salió bien||
*Por culpa de* blames. When things go well, thank with *gracias a*.
p:por-la-manana: Almost. After a clock time, Spanish uses *de*, not *por*.
Keep the *la*: *mañana* on its own means tomorrow.
The day takes *el*, and the part of the day takes *por la*.
p:por-lo-general: por lo generales los clientes llegan temprano||
Almost. The phrase is fixed: *general* never changes to a plural.
por general los clientes llegan temprano||
Almost. You need *lo* in the middle: *por lo general*.
Almost. *Siempre* means no exceptions, so it fights with *salvo excepciones*.
p:por-orden-de: se atiende por orden de la llegada||
Almost. After *por orden de* the criterion stays bare, with no *la*.
se atiende en orden de llegada||
Almost. The fixed phrase uses *por*, not *en*.
Almost. You need *de* before the criterion.
p:por-que-no: Almost. The question is two words with an accent, *por qué*; *porque* is because.
por qué no fuimos a monserrate||
In the past it's a real question about something that didn't happen. To suggest, use the present.
por qué no descansar un rato||
Advice speaks to someone, so the verb needs their ending: *descansas*.
p:por-todo-lo-anterior-solicito: por todo lo anterior solicito devolver el dinero||
Almost. You want someone else to act, so use *que* and the subjunctive.
por todos los anteriores solicito el reembolso del pago||
Almost. *Por todo lo anterior* is a fixed phrase and never changes.
por todo lo anterior quiero mi dinero||
Almost. *Quiero* sounds blunt in a formal letter, and a deadline makes the demand stronger.
p:posicion-precisa: la cocina está al fondo el pasillo||
Almost. Keep the *de*, and with *el* it becomes *del*.
hay un parque frente el edificio||
*Frente* needs *a* before the place, and *a* plus *el* becomes *al*.
Almost. *Alrededor* needs *de* before the place: *alrededor de la casa*.
p:position-de: la droguería está al lado de el banco||
el parqueadero está detrás el edificio||
The *de* is part of the phrase: *detrás de*, here *detrás del*.
vivo entre de la panadería y el café||
*Entre* is the one that takes no *de*.
p:possessives-basic: The -s follows the things: several friends, so *mis*.
*Tú* with an accent means you. Your is *tu*, no accent.
tomás y vale trabajan en sus café||
Two people, but one café, so *su*. The -s follows the things, not the owners.
p:postura: estuve en los pies todo el día||
Almost. Spanish uses the fixed phrase *de pie* for standing, not a phrase about feet.
Spanish says which way the face points: *boca arriba*, not "on the back".
The phrase starts with *de*, as in *de pie* and *de lado*.
p:precisamente-concretamente: Almost. The spotlight word goes right before the phrase it points at.
necesito ayuda concreto con la cocina||
Almost. The adverb ends in *-mente*; *concreto* alone is an adjective.
p:preferir-a: prefiero el té que el café||
Almost. *Preferir* compares with *a*, like English to; *que* belongs to *más que*.
prefiero el té a el café||
When you'd rather someone else did it, the verb takes the wishing form: *decidas*.
p:preferiria-que: preferiría que fuimos a otro sitio||
Almost. After *preferiría que* you need the *-ra* form, *fuéramos*, not the plain past.
me preferiría que quedar en casa||
Almost. When you are the one doing it, there is no *que*: just the infinitive.
prefiero que fuéramos a otro sitio|yo|
Almost. The soft "I'd rather" is *preferiría*; plain *prefiero* does not go with the *-ra* form.
p:prefieres-x-o-y: *Nosotros* is outside the boot, and it's an *-ir* verb: *preferimos*.
An either-or question wants one of the two, not yes.
p:prefiero-que-a-que: prefiero que me dicen la verdad||
Almost. After *prefiero que*, the verb takes its "other" ending, so *dicen* becomes *digan*.
prefiero que me llames que me escribas||
Almost. English "than" becomes *a que* in this pattern, so a bare *que* between the two halves is not enough.
prefiero que yo me quede en casa a que yo salga||
Almost. When one person chooses and does, Spanish uses the infinitive instead of repeating "I".
p:preguntar-pedir: le pedí dónde queda la estación||
Almost. Where something is, is an answer, so it's *preguntar*.
Spanish doesn't ask a question, it makes one: *hacer una pregunta*.
The person you ask always gets *le*, even a woman.
p:prep-questions-basic: Spanish never leaves *de* at the end. It goes in front of *dónde*.
In a question, why is two words with an accent: *por qué*. *Porque* is the answer.
p:presentation-frame: os voy a hablar de bogotá||hoy
Almost. *Os* is from Spain; in Latin America, to you all is always *les*.
primero lugar el café tiene 100 años||
It needs *en* in front, and *primero* shortens to *primer* before *lugar*.
para terminar les voy mostrar unas fotos||
Going to do something is always *voy a*, so don't drop the *a*.
p:presente-narrativo: voy por la calle y me encontré a hernando||ayer
Almost. Pick one tense for the story and stay in it.
estoy yendo al mercado y me encuentro a hernando||ayer
Almost. English likes "I'm going", but Spanish uses the simple present.
entro a la oficina y todos quedan callados||
Almost. "Go quiet" is *quedarse callado*, so keep the *se*.
p:presenting-to-audience: como puedes ver en la pantalla las ventas bajaron||
Almost. *Puedes* is for one friend; a group is *ustedes*, so *pueden*.
a continuación los voy a presentar los resultados||
Almost. *Los* would be "them"; to say "to you all" you need *les*.
Almost. This is a fixed phrase and it ends in *-a*.
p:presuntamente-al-parecer: Almost. *Presuntamente* is for accusations, so for everyday "apparently" use *al parecer*.
según fuentes de la fiscalía el concejal recibió dinero||
The plain past makes the paper vouch for it, while the conditional keeps its distance.
al parecer que el incendio empezó en la cocina||
No *que* after *al parecer*, which works like the English "apparently".
p:prever-prevenir: Almost. *Previno* is *prevenir*, so it says nobody stopped it; to say nobody saw it coming, use *previó*.
The saying is about acting early so there is nothing to cure, and that is *prevenir*.
Almost. *Prever* follows *ver*, so its participle is *previsto*, like *visto*.
p:proceder-de: "Comes from" is always *de*, whatever the place.
One word takes *proviene*, several words take *provienen*.
la iglesia se remonta en el siglo xvi||
p:propio-de: esa actitud no es propio de un profesional||
Almost. *Propio* agrees with what it describes, and *actitud* is feminine.
estas lluvias son propias a abril||
es un plato propia de la costa||
Almost. *Plato* is masculine, so you need *propio*.
p:provocar-ocasionar: Almost. The verb agrees with the cause, and *declaraciones* is plural.
el incendio fue provocado de un cigarrillo||
*Porque* needs a whole clause. With just a noun for the cause, use a verb like *causar*.
p:puedo-hacerte-una-pregunta: Almost. *Te* attaches to the end of the infinitive as one word: *hacerte*.
Almost. In Spanish you *hacer* a question, and *preguntar* is for the thing you want to know.
te puedo hacer una pregunta doctor||
Almost. *Te* is for friends; with someone you call *usted*, switch to *le* and the softer *podría*.
p:pues-claro-que: Almost. To sound mildly offended, add *pues* and repeat the verb without *sí*.
te aseguro que no fui señor|yo|
Almost. Speaking to *usted* you need *le*, not *te*.
Almost. When you give something to him or her, *le la* becomes *se la*.
p:quantifiers-basic: *Trabajo* is a thing, and you count things with *mucho*. *Muy* only goes before a describing word.
Very well is *muy bien*. *Mucho* never sits in front of *bien*.
Before a thing, *mucho* takes its ending: *preguntas* needs *muchas*.
p:que-no-dice-que-si: mi mamá dice si vienes a almorzar||
Almost. English says "asks whether" with no "that", but after *dice* Spanish needs the *que* first.
mi mamá dice que sí vienes a almorzar||
Almost. With the accent, *sí* is "yes" and the sentence is no longer a question.
p:que-opinas-de-que: qué opinas de que cierran la biblioteca||
Almost. You are reacting to the event, not reporting it, so the verb after *de que* flips to the subjunctive.
qué opinas que hayan cerrado la biblioteca||
p:que-opinas-de: Almost. You ask *what* someone thinks, not *how*: *qué*.
qué piensas de el nuevo alcalde||
p:que-si-que-si: Almost. You don't need to say "I said"; the bare *que* does that.
que si mamá que te llamo||ya
Almost. This *sí* means "yes", so it needs its accent.
Almost. Repeating *que no* sounds impatient, so with a stranger use *ya le dije*.
p:que-subj-deseo: Almost. After *que*, a wish takes the subjunctive: *diviertas*.
Without *que* the wish falls apart; say *Que te diviertas* or *Diviértete*.
Pick one shape: *Diviértete* on its own, or *Que te diviertas*.
p:que-subj-me-parece: que lo han despedido me parece injusto||
Almost. You're judging the news, not just reporting it, so the verb after *que* is subjunctive.
que cierren el café me parece tristemente||
After *parece* Spanish uses an adjective, like English seems sad, not an adverb.
lo hayan despedido me parece injusto||
The *que* is what opens the fact, like the fact that in English, so it has to stay.
p:que-subj-repeated-order: Almost. After *que*, drop the command form and use the subjunctive: *te calles*.
Almost. *Vienes* is a plain fact; *vengas* is the order.
que cierres la puerta por favor||
Almost. *Que* is for the second try. The first time, give a plain polite order.
p:que-tal-si: English says how about going. Spanish says how about if we go: *si vamos*.
Almost. *Si* wants a real verb with a person in it: *vamos*.
qué tal sí vamos a cine||
This *si* means if, so no accent. *Sí* with an accent is yes.
p:que-tipo-de: qué tipo de la música te gusta||
No *el* or *la* after *tipo de*: it names a kind.
qué tipo de películas te gusta||
The verb agrees with *películas*, which is plural.
p:que-x-este: Almost. In this exclamation the demonstrative goes after the noun.
Almost. The demonstrative must match the noun: *mujer* is feminine, so *esta*.
p:queda-por-resolver: Almost. The verb agrees with what is left, and there is one problem.
queda por ser resuelto el problema||
Almost. Spanish keeps a plain infinitive here; no *ser* + participle is needed.
queda a resolver si el efecto dura||
Almost. The phrase always uses *por*, not *a*.
p:quedar-a-distancia: Almost. For distance Spanish uses *a*, not *en*.
mi casa queda a 2 cuadras el café||
Almost. After the distance you need *de*, and *de* plus *el* becomes *del*.
Almost. To ask how far, keep the *a*: *¿A cuánto queda…?*
p:quedar-cerca: el banco es cerca del parque||
Almost. Where something is never takes *es*. Use *queda* or *está*.
*Queda* is for places that don't move. People take *está*.
p:quedar-en: Almost. English says agreed to, but here Spanish uses *en*.
nos quedamos en vernos a las 8||
