*Quedarse* means to stay. To agree on a plan, use plain *quedar*, with no *nos* in front.
quedamos que tú traías la torta||
The *en* stays in front of *que*, even though English drops it.
p:quedar-faltar-sobrar: Almost. The verb agrees with the thing that's missing, and ten chairs is plural.
In English you are the one who's short. In Spanish the chairs are missing, and you only get a small word in front: *me*, *nos*.
*Sobrar* means too many. If you need more, the verb is *faltar*.
p:quedar-grabado: Almost. The image is what stays engraved, so it is the subject and you are only *me*.
la imagen se me quedó grabado||
Almost. *Grabada* must agree with *la imagen*, which is feminine.
esas tardes se nos quedó grabadas||
Almost. Two afternoons mean a plural verb: *quedaron*.
p:quedar-participio: Almost. The describing word agrees with the noun, and *casa* is feminine.
The verb goes plural with the buildings.
*Resolver* has an irregular result word, *resuelto*, like *volver* and *vuelto*.
p:queria-cortesia: *Quiero* is correct but blunt. With a stranger, *quería* is the polite step back.
*Quise* is a finished past, so it sounds like you tried once and gave up. The polite step back is *quería*.
English says *I was wondering*, but Spanish needs no *estaba*: plain *quería* already sounds soft.
p:question-word-order: After the question word comes the verb, then the person.
Spanish has no does. The verb itself carries the question.
p:quien-tuviera: Almost. The wish needs the *-ra* form; *tengo* is just "I have".
Almost. Wishes use the *-ra* form, not the *-ría* "would" form.
p:quieres-decir-que: Almost. *Quieres decir* needs *que* before the claim.
qué quieres decir que no vienes||
Almost. *¿Qué quieres decir?* means "what do you mean?"; to check a claim, drop the *qué*.
Almost. *Quiere* is for *usted*, so with a friend use *quieres*.
p:recien-participio: Almost. The participle matches the noun: *cocina* is feminine, so *pintada*.
Almost. To say you just arrived, use the past: *recién llegué*.
p:recordar-acordarse: Almost. *Recordar* takes the thing directly, with no *de*.
*Acordarse* always needs its *de* before the thing you remember.
acordé de que era su cumpleaños||
Without *me*, *acordar* means to agree on something. To remember, you need the *me/te/se*.
p:rectificar-reparar: Almost. A phone is a thing to fix, and *rectificar* is for words and figures; use *arreglar* or *reparar*.
Almost. English says "fix" for anything, but statements get corrected with *rectificar*.
el senador admitió de su error||
Almost. English says "admit to", but *admitir* takes the mistake directly, with no *de*.
p:refuse-es-que: Careful. *No quiero* on its own sounds like you don't like the person. Give a cushion and a reason.
Almost. English says it's because; Spanish excuses start with plain *es que*.
True, but cold. Wrap the fact in a cushion and offer another day.
p:renunciar-a: Almost. *Renunciar* needs *a* before what you give up.
Almost. English "from" tempts you, but Spanish uses *a*.
p:repartir-entre: repartieron la herencia en los hijos||
Almost. When the people who receive are named, Spanish uses *entre*, not *en*.
partimos la cuenta en la mitad||
Almost. English says "in half", but Spanish says *por la mitad*.
Almost. The parts you end up with follow *en*.
p:repeticion-claro-claro: Almost. Repeat the same word, don't change it the second time.
Almost. The trick is the exact same word twice. Mixing in another word breaks the echo.
p:reporting-verbs-stance: Almost. Reporting verbs take *que* directly; there is no *de* before it.
dijo que reconoció que se había equivocado|él|
Almost. *Reconoció que* already means "he said, admitting", so you don't need *dijo que* as well.
Almost. If he never said it outright, *dijo* is too strong; *insinuó* says he only hinted.
p:reproach-questions: Almost. English puts "for" at the end; Spanish moves it to the front as *a* and joins the action with *para*.
Spanish needs *para* before the thing you should be doing.
me cayó muy mal que no me invitaste||
After *me cayó mal que*, the verb takes the *-aras* ending, not the plain past *invitaste*.
p:request-ladder: me hace el favor cerrar la puerta||
Almost. The favour needs *de* before the action.
After *puede*, the action stays in its basic *-r* form.
To a stranger, a bare friend command sounds bossy. Use *usted* and ask: *¿Me puede...?*
p:resistente-a: Almost. The threat follows *a*, not *de*, and *a el* becomes *al*.
The verb *resistir* takes its object directly, while the adjective *resistente* needs *a*.
p:resulta-adj-que: resulta absurdo que nadie se dio cuenta antes||
Almost. You are judging the fact, not just reporting it, so the verb is subjunctive.
resulta raro de que vale no venga||hoy
Almost. Spanish links with plain *que*, no *de*.
a la larga resulta más barato reparar de comprar||
Almost. Comparing two things takes *que*, as in "cheaper than".
p:resultar-ser: Almost. The adjective agrees with the thing described: *noticia* is feminine.
The verb needs to be plural too.
la noticia resultó a ser falsa||
English says *turned out to be*, but Spanish puts *ser* straight after *resultó*, with no *a*.
p:romperse-la-cabeza: rompí mi cabeza tratando de entenderlo||
Almost. Spanish puts the owner in the pronoun *me*, so the head becomes *la cabeza*.
me rompí la cabeza a entenderlo||
Almost. English "trying to" becomes *tratando de* or *pensando en*.
Almost. A negative command to a friend swaps the vowel: *romper* gives *rompas*, not *rompes*.
p:rozar-el-ridiculo: el final roza en el ridículo||
Almost. English says "borders on", but *rozar* needs no preposition.
Almost. The noun keeps its article, *el*.
Almost. For an adjective used as an idea, add *lo*: *lo absurdo*.
p:saber-conocer: English says know how to; Spanish puts the verb straight after *sé*.
A place you could visit goes with *conocer*.
p:salir-a-la-luz: la verdad salió a luz años después||
Almost. The phrase is *a la luz*, with *la*; plain *a luz* belongs to *dar a luz*, to give birth.
mariana salió a la luz el escándalo||
Almost. When someone brings a thing out, Spanish uses *sacar*, not *salir*.
el escándalo sacó a la luz el lunes||
Almost. A scandal does not bring anything out; it comes out, so *salió*.
p:salir-adelante: Almost. *En adelante* means "from now on"; for pulling through, use *adelante* alone.
Almost. *Adelante* never takes an ending, even with several people.
Almost. To say what you survived, put *a pesar de* before it.
p:salirle-bien: la entrevista fue bien para mí||
Almost. English says *went well for me*, but Spanish puts the person up front: *me fue bien*.
The verb agrees with the things that turned out, so plural things need *salieron*.
The exam is what went, not you: *te fue*, like *gustar*.
p:saltar-a-la-vista: salta a la vista de que no ensayaron||
Almost. English "obvious that" has no extra word, and neither does Spanish: plain *que*.
salta a la vista que no ensayaran||
Almost. It is a plain fact you can see, so the verb stays in the ordinary past, with no subjunctive.
salta en la vista que no ensayaron||
Almost. The set phrase is *a la vista*, and it does not change.
p:saludos-de-mi-parte: Almost. *Hola* is the word you say; what you pass on are *saludos*.
dale saludos a tu mamá de mí||
Almost. "From me" is *de mi parte*, never *de mí*.
dale saludos a su esposa de mi parte||
Almost. With *usted*, the command is *dele*, not *dale*.
p:same-subject-haber: no recuerdo que yo firmé eso||
Almost. When the same person did it, Spanish skips the *que* clause and uses *haber*.
estoy segura haber cerrado la puerta||
Almost. After *haber*, the verb takes its *-do* ending: *firmado*.
p:se-divide-en: el libro se divide a 3 partes||
el edificio se compone en 4 pisos||
se le llama el café negro tinto||
Spanish puts the name first, then *a* plus the thing named.
p:se-entiende-por: Almost. *Consistir* takes *en* and explains what something involves; for listing parts, use *constar de*.
se entiende por economía informal es el conjunto de actividades||
Almost. After *se entiende por*, the term goes straight into the definition without *es*.
el jurado se compone en 5 miembros||
Almost. *Componerse* takes *de*, not *en*, before the parts.
p:se-me-body: Almost. Spanish puts the person in *me* and gives the body part *el*, not *mi*.
se me pusieron mis pelos de punta||
Almost. The *me* already says whose hair it is, so use *los*.
se me puso los pelos de punta||
Almost. The verb agrees with the body part, and *los pelos* is plural.
p:se-me-involuntary: Almost. *Me* already says whose eyes they are, so use *los*, not *mis*.
Almost. The verb agrees with the body part, and *los ojos* is plural.
Almost. *Se* always comes first, then *me*, *te* or *le*.
p:se-podria-objetar-que: se podría objetar de que el proyecto es caro||
Almost. English speakers add a little preposition here; Spanish goes straight to *que*.
se podría objetar que sea caro||
Almost. You are stating what the objector would claim, so the verb stays ordinary: *es*.
se podría objetar que el proyecto es caro||
An objection with no answer leaves your opponent the last word, so follow it with *Sin embargo*.
p:se-puede-me-dejas: Almost. *Se puede* asks about a rule; when one person decides, ask *me dejas*.
After *se puede* the verb stays in the infinitive: *fumar*.
After *dejar* the infinitive comes straight away, with no *a*.
p:se-reciproco: Almost. *Nos* already means each other; there's nothing to add.
rosa y hernando conocieron en el café||
Without *se*, met has no one to meet; *se* says they met each other.
*Les* points at other people; for each other, use *se*.
p:se-ruega: se ruega a los asistentes apaguen el celular||
Almost. When you name who is asked, *que* has to introduce the request.
se ruega no fuman en las instalaciones||
Almost. After *se ruega no*, the verb stays an infinitive.
se ruega a los asistentes que apagan el celular||
Almost. After *que* in a request, the verb takes the subjunctive: *apaguen*.
p:se-trata-de: la película se trata de una familia||
Almost. You will hear this a lot, but in careful writing the named thing is the subject, so *se* drops out: *la película trata de*.
se trata una oferta de altamira||
The *de* is part of the phrase: it is always *se trata de*.
es sobre una oferta de altamira||
Almost. English says "it's about", but to say what a situation is about, Spanish uses *se trata de*.
p:seguir-gerundio: Almost. After *seguir* Spanish wants the *-ndo* form, not the infinitive.
For "still not", swap *no* for *sin* and use the infinitive.
sigo a trabajar en el café||
No *a* is needed. The *-ndo* form carries the whole idea.
p:seguir-por: siga a lo largo de la séptima hasta la calle 72||
Close. *A lo largo de* is a word-for-word *along*. Giving directions, Spanish just says *por*.
iba en la caracas cuando pasó||
Almost. *En* is for a fixed spot; when you are moving along a road, Spanish uses *por*.
en colombia se maneja en la derecha||
Almost. English says *on the right*, but the side you travel on takes *por* in Spanish.
p:segun-dicen: según mariana dice que el acta no está||
Almost. *Según Mariana* already means "Mariana says", so *dice que* repeats it.
Almost. The news after *parece que* is an ordinary statement, with no special verb form.
según dicen que altamira quiere comprar toda la cuadra||
Almost. *Según dicen* is a marker, not "they say that", so no *que* follows.
p:seguramente-probablemente: Almost. *Probablemente* works on its own, like *maybe*: no *es* and no *que* in front of it.
seguramente hernando está aquí lo sé||
Almost. English "surely" sounds certain, but *seguramente* only means most likely. If you know, say it without the guess word.
Almost. *Probablemente* takes the subjunctive freely. *A lo mejor* almost never does.
p:sembrar-la-duda: Almost. The phrase needs *en*: *poner en duda*.
Almost. English says "make" or "ask", but Spanish raises a doubt with *plantear*.
estoy sembrando dudas sobre el contrato||
Almost. *Sembrar* means causing doubt in others; for your own doubts, use *tener dudas*.
p:sencillamente: *Sencilla* means easy; to say simply perfect you need the *-mente* word.
*Simple* is an adjective; the word for simply is *simplemente*.
p:senor-don-article: When you speak to someone, *señor* stands alone.
Talking about him needs the *el*: *el señor Ruiz*.
el don hernando llega a las 7||
p:sentir-lo-de: Almost. After *siento*, use the plain infinitive.
You need *lo de*. It is the bridge to the news.
siento que te tienes que ir||
To say you are sorry, use the *tengas* form. *Siento que tienes que irte* means "I feel you have to leave".
p:sentirse-mal: Almost. For how you feel, use *mal*; *malo* describes a person or a thing.
Without *me*, the verb loses you; add *me* to talk about how you feel.
Before an adjective Spanish says *muy*, not *mucho*.
p:ser-bueno-para: Almost. English says good *at*, but Spanish reaches for *para*.
mi hermana es bueno para los idiomas||
*Bueno* matches the person, so for a woman it is *buena*.
*Bien* says how you do something. To describe a person, use *bueno*.
p:ser-capaz-de: no fui capaz decirle la verdad||
Almost. English drops the little word, but *capaz* always needs *de* before the infinitive.
Close. The adjective agrees with the people: plural *capaces*.
*Ser capaz de* is about nerve or what someone would do. For plain skill, use *saber* or *poder*.
p:ser-de-material: Almost. Spanish needs *de* before the material.
el suéter es de una lana||
Close. No article after *de* here: *de lana*.
The material comes after the noun, with *de*: *un bolso de cuero*.
p:ser-event-location: To ask where an event takes place, Spanish uses *ser*.
el café es en la candelaria||
A place or thing takes *estar* for its location.
p:ser-profession-no-article: Naming what you do takes no *un* or *una*.
No article, and the job changes for a woman.
With an opinion about him, *un* comes back.
p:ser-un-acierto: fue un acierto cambiando de director||
Almost. Spanish uses the infinitive here, not the *-ando* form that English *-ing* suggests.
fue una acierto abrir la terraza||
fue un acierto que abrir la terraza||
Almost. The infinitive follows directly, with no *que*.
p:ser-un-duro: es una duro para las matemáticas||
Almost. The noun has to match the person, so a woman is *una dura*.
Almost. Without *un* or *una*, *es duro* means that something is hard, not that someone is good.
es un duro de las matemáticas||
p:ser-un-noun: vale es una genia para los postres||
Almost. *Genio* keeps its own *un*, even when you mean a woman.
Keep the little word: the noun is the verdict, so it needs *una* in front.
hernando es un genio de manejar||
To say what someone is brilliant at, Spanish uses *para*.
p:seria-posible: sería posible que cambiar la cita||
Almost. With *que* you need a verb with an ending; without a new person, just use the infinitive.
es posible que me enviara el documento||hoy
Almost. *Sería* is what makes it polite; *es* with the *-ra* form clashes.
me podría confirmar que la reserva sigue en pie||
Almost. When you are unsure, "whether" is *si*, not *que*.
p:serias-tan-amable: sería tan amable para bajar el volumen||
Almost. The frame is *tan amable de*, with *de*, not *para*.
sería mucho pedir que cierras la puerta||
Almost. After *sería mucho pedir que* use the past subjunctive, *cerraras*.
tendría la bondad esperar un momento||
Almost. *La bondad* needs *de* before the verb.
p:servir-para: Almost. After *para*, the verb keeps its basic form: *abrir*.
English leaves "for" at the end; Spanish puts *para qué* at the front.
*trabajar* is for people. For a phone that doesn't work, Colombians say *no sirve*.
p:si-algo-es: si algo tengo claro es no vuelvo||
Almost. A whole sentence after *es* needs *que*.
si de algo estoy seguro es la honestidad de hernando||
Almost. The preposition comes back: *de algo… es de…*.
si algo me gusta de este barrio es de su gente||
Almost. *Gustar* doesn't need *de* in front of the spotlight, so don't add one.
p:si-bien-no-olvidemos: si bien es cierto que el proyecto es caro pero no olvidemos que generará empleo||
Almost. The second phrase already does the job of *pero*.
si bien es cierto que el proyecto sea caro no olvidemos que generará empleo||
Almost. You are granting something true, so *es cierto que* takes the ordinary form.
si bien es cierto el proyecto es caro no olvidemos generará empleo||
Almost. Both halves need their *que*, unlike the little "that" English likes to drop.
p:si-pero-que: sí pero que no se entera tu papá||
Almost. After *sí, pero que* Spanish wants the subjunctive (*entere*), not the plain *entera*.
listo que estás de vuelta antes de medianoche||siempre
A condition is not a fact yet, so the verb after *siempre que* takes *estés*.
sí pero no que se entere tu papá||
The *que* comes first and *no* goes right before the verb.
p:si-quieres-que: Almost. After *que* the verb takes its subjunctive: *vaya*, not *va*.
Almost. To the person in front of you, use the plain command; *que* is for someone else.
si se lo quiere decir que diga se lo||
Almost. The pronouns go before the verb: *que se lo diga*.
p:si-solo-si-siempre-y-cuando: te puedes llevar el carro y cuando lo devuelves con gasolina||siempre
Almost. *Siempre y cuando* needs the subjunctive: *devuelvas*.
sí pero solo si termines la tarea||
*Solo si* works like the ordinary *si*, so there is no subjunctive.
Keep the *que*: *salvo que* works as one unit.
p:si-volviera-a-nacer: si volvería a nacer estudiaría otra cosa||
Almost. The *si* part takes the subjunctive, never the conditional.
si volviera a nacer estudio otra cosa||
Almost. The result needs the conditional, because it is imagined.
si podía devolver el tiempo le diría que la quiero||
Almost. For something unreal, use *pudiera*, not *podía*.
p:si-yo-no-fui: Almost. English says "it wasn't me", but Spanish says "I didn't (do it)": *yo no fui*.
Almost. The blame is about something that already happened, so use the past *fui*.
p:siempre-gerundio: Almost. English 'always to arrive' tempts the dictionary form, but the outburst needs the -ing form, *llegando*.
Almost. *Quejarse* needs its little word, *-te* for you or *-me* for me, so we know who is complaining.
p:siento-llegar-tarde: Almost. After *siento*, use the dictionary form: *llegar*, not *llego*.
When you name what you did, drop the *lo*: just *Siento llegar tarde*.
lo siento dónde está el baño||
To get someone's attention, *disculpe* or *perdón*. *Lo siento* is for real regret.
p:siento-mucho-que: siento mucho que no puedes venir||
After a feeling about someone else, the next verb is subjunctive: *puedas*, not *puedes*.
Before *que* Spanish drops *lo*: *Lo siento* stands alone, *siento que* leads into the reason.
siento mucho que tuviste que esperar||
For something that already happened, use *hayas* plus the participle, not an ordinary past tense.
p:siento-no-haber: siento que no te avisé antes||
Almost. When you are the one who did it, Spanish uses *haber* and the *-ado* form, not a second clause.
Almost. The pronoun attaches to the end of *haber*.
Almost. After *haber* comes the *-ado* form, not the infinitive.
p:sin-animo-de: sin ánimo contradecirlo creo que hay un error||
Almost. The phrase needs *de* before the verb.
sin ánimo de ofendo ese precio me parece alto||
Almost. After *de* Spanish uses the infinitive, not a conjugated form.
puede que me equivoco pero falta un dato||
Almost. *Puede que* is followed by the subjunctive, *equivoque*.
p:sin-rumbo-fijo: salimos sin rumbo a la plaza||
Almost. If you know the place, it is *con rumbo a*; *sin rumbo* means you do not.
Almost. After *sin* Spanish drops the article: *sin rumbo fijo*, like "aimlessly".
el bus sale con rumbo en medellín||
p:sintiendolo-mucho: tengo miedo que no voy a poder||
Almost. *Tengo miedo* is real fear; *me temo que* is the polite "I'm afraid".
sintiendo mucho me resulta imposible acompañarte||
You need the little *lo* ("it") on the end, and the accent that goes with it.
A bare no still sounds cold, so add the real reason.
p:sobre-todo-solo: me gusta el deporte solo el fútbol||
With *solo* you'd like football and nothing else. To keep the rest and single one out, use *sobre todo*.
If you never drink it later, that's *only*: *solo*. *Sobre todo* would mean mostly in the morning.
*Voy solo* means you're going alone. For *I'm the only one going*, start with *solo*: *solo voy yo*.
p:sobre-todo: me gusta el barrio sobretodo la gente||
Almost. It is two words; *sobretodo* is a wrong spelling.
me gustan los deportes sobre todos el fútbol||
Almost. The phrase never changes: *todo* stays singular.
me gustan los deportes sobre todo y el fútbol||
Almost. No *y* is needed; the standout case follows straight after.
p:sobrevivir-a: You will hear it without *a*, but *sobrevivir a* is the safe, standard form.
la empresa sobrevivió de la crisis||
English "survive" has no little word, but Spanish wants *a*, not *de*.
For things that hold up under pressure, such as a bridge or a roof, Spanish says *resistir*.
p:soler-inf: Almost. After *suelo*, the second verb stays in its dictionary form.
The o only turns to ue in *suelo, sueles, suele, suelen*; with we it's *solemos*.
Nothing goes between *suelo* and the second verb.
p:solicitamos-su-colaboracion: solicitamos su colaboración a llenar el formulario||
Almost. What the help is for is introduced by *para*.
solicitamos su colaboración para llenando el formulario||
Almost. English says "in filling", but after *para* Spanish uses the infinitive.
vale solicito su colaboración para mover la mesa||
Almost. That formula is far too stiff for a friend; just say *¿me ayudas?*.
p:solicitar: solicito para una cita con la directora||
Almost. *Solicitar* takes what you want directly, with no *para*.
solicitamos su autorización usar su nombre||
Almost. *Para* links the permission to what it is for.
Almost. *Solicito* belongs on paper; at a counter you ask with *¿me regala…?*.
p:solo-que: el plan es bueno pero solo que es caro||
Almost. *Solo que* already does the job of *pero*, so you don't need both.
English says "I just can't", but Spanish needs the *que* to join the second sentence.
p:somos-cuatro: hay 5 de nosotros en mi familia||
Almost. Spanish has no of us here: just *somos* and the number.
son 4 en mi familia mis papás mi hermana y yo||
If you're in the group, it's *somos*, not *son*.
p:sonar-con-ganas: Almost. English says *dream of*, but Spanish says *con*.
Don't drop *con*: you dream with it.
p:sonar-con: sueño de vivir junto al mar||
Almost. English says *dream of*, but Spanish says *dream with*: *soñar con*.
The vowel changes when the stress falls on it: *sueño*, but *soñamos*.
mi sueño es de tener una finca||
After *es*, go straight to the infinitive. No extra word.
p:sostener-que: el alcalde sostiene de que nunca firmó el contrato||
Almost. Spanish does not add *de* before *que* here.
mantuvo su versión pese de las pruebas||
Almost. The fixed phrase is *pese a*.
Almost. After *que*, the claim needs a verb with its own ending.
p:street-names: la oficina queda en la calle de 72||
Almost. No *de* between *calle* and its number or name.
Say *en la* before the street, and join the two streets with *con*.
la oficina es en la carrera séptima||
Where a place is never takes *es*; use *queda* or *está*.
p:subir-subida: hay un aumento de las ventas||
Almost. For something that already happened, use *hubo*.
Almost. After a verb of change, the amount comes with *un*, not *de*.
p:subirse-bajarse: Almost. You get off *de* the vehicle, so *del bus*.
Getting on needs the little *me*, and the vehicle takes *a*: *al bus*.
*Tomar* works everywhere. Colombians say *coger* too, but in Mexico and Argentina it's a rude word, so *tomo el bus* is the safe habit.
p:supongo-imagino-tag: Almost. At the front, Spanish needs *que*: *supongo que…*. Only the tag at the end stands alone.
Almost. The ending already says "I", so *yo* only makes it sound like you are arguing.
Almost. The guess is yours, so it is *supongo*, not the *tú* form.
p:surgir-de: mi familia es originaria en cartagena||
Almost. The place of origin comes after *de*, not *en*.
el proyecto fue surgido de una conversación||
Almost. *Surgir* has no passive: the project simply *surgió*.
la costumbre se remonta desde la época colonial||
Almost. *Remontarse* points back *a* a time; English "from" does not carry over.
p:suspended-intensifier: Almost. For a story about yesterday, use the past form *hacía*.
*Hambre* is feminine but takes *un* in the singular, like *el agua*.
Here *nervios* is plural, so it matches *unos*.
p:synonym-hypernym: tomás compró un carro viejo pero el carro no arrancó||
Correct, but clumsy in writing: use a synonym or a broader word instead of repeating.
rosa nos contó todo no lo esperábamos de una mujer tan discreto||
The describing word follows the person: a woman needs *discreta*.
vale hizo una torta y la postre se acabó rápido||
Almost. *Postre* is masculine, even though *torta* is feminine.
p:talla-numero: Almost. With *calzar*, *número* is the natural word: *¿Qué número calza?*
Close. *Tamaño* is size in general, like a big box; for clothes it's *talla*.
Nearly. Several trainers, so the verb is *quedan*.
p:tambien-tampoco: There's no '*no también*' in Spanish. Agreeing with a no-sentence is *tampoco*.
*Yo también* after a no-sentence sounds like 'I do speak it'.
p:tardar-en: Almost. The action after the time takes *en*, not *para*.
me tarda una hora en llegar||
*Tardar* doesn't work like *gustar*. You're the one taking the time, so it's *tardo*, with no *me*.
Don't drop the *en*: it links the time to the action.
p:te-habria-gustado-que: Almost. *Gustar* stays in the third person; *te* says who likes it.
te habría gustado que te lo habría contado||
After *que*, the second verb takes *hubiera*, not *habría*.
te gustaría estudiar otra carrera asking about back then||
*Gustaría* looks forward. To ask about the past, add *haber*.
p:te-importa-si: te importa si abra la ventana||
Almost. After *si* use the plain present, not a subjunctive.
Say who it might bother: add *te* or *le*.
te importo si abro la ventana||
The thing that bothers is the situation, not you, so the verb is *importa*.
p:te-importaria-inf: Almost. *Importar* works like *gustar*: the job bothers you, so the person is *te*, not *tú*.
Almost. Strictly, *sí* here means "yes, I mind". When you are happy to, start with *no* so it is clear.
Almost. English says "mind closing", but Spanish uses the dictionary form *cerrar*.
p:te-importaria-que: te importaría que abro la ventana||
After *importaría* the verb takes the *-ra* form, not the plain present.
te importa que abriera la ventana||
Mixing the two is the slip. Either *¿Te importa que abra...?* or the softer *¿Te importaría que abriera...?*: *importaría* goes with *-ra*.
Almost. "Sí" would mean "yes, it bothers me"; to say "go ahead", say *no*.
p:te-importaria: Almost. The one who might mind is the person you're asking: *te*, not *me*.
English says waiting, but Spanish always uses the dictionary form here: *esperar*.
A plain *sí* answers the question as asked: yes, I'd mind. To say you're glad to help, start with *no*.
p:te-invito-a: The person you invite is *te*, and it goes before the verb.
*Te gustas* means you like yourself. The invitation is *te gustaría*.
p:te-lo-agradezco: Almost. *Agradecer* already carries the meaning "for", so the thing follows with no *por*.
Almost. After thanks, the reason is introduced by *por*, never *para*.
Almost. The person comes first: *te lo*, never *lo te*.
p:te-parece-bien-que: te parece bien que nos vemos a las 8||
Almost. After *te parece bien que*, use the subjunctive: *veamos*.
es bien para ti que nos veamos a las 8||
Almost. *Is it OK with you* isn't built word for word: Spanish asks *¿te parece bien...?*
p:te-presento-a: Almost. Before a person Spanish needs *a*; without it Vale sounds like a parcel.
te presento a el señor gómez||
For a woman it's *esta*; *este* is for a man.
*Introducir* means to put in or insert. To introduce a person, use *presentar*.
p:te-propongo-que: te propongo que vamos al cine||
Almost. A proposal tries to move people, so the verb after *que* takes the "asking" ending.
te propongo a ir al cine||
Almost. *Proponer* takes the infinitive directly, with no *a*.
Almost. Name who you are proposing to with *te*, *le* or *les*.
p:telling-time: Almost. One o'clock is singular, so it takes *es la*.
Close. More than one hour is plural: *son las tres*.
p:ten-cuidado-con: Almost. The thing to watch out for follows *con*.
English uses "-ing"; Spanish uses *al* plus the infinitive.
A warning is a command, so *ten*, not the plain *tienes*.
p:tendrias-que: Almost. "You'd have to" needs *que* before the infinitive.
Almost. *Deberías* goes straight into the infinitive, with no *que*.
yo que tú voy al médico||
Almost. After *yo que tú*, use the "would" form: *iría*, not *voy*.
p:tener-anos: Almost. In Spanish you have your years: *tengo*.
Ask how many years you have: *¿Cuántos años tienes?*
p:tener-buena-mano: tiene buen mano para las plantas||
Almost. *Mano* is feminine, so it needs *buena*.
es buena mano para las plantas||
Almost. A knack is something you have, so Spanish uses *tener*, not *ser*.
tiene buena mano a las plantas||
p:tener-el-gusto-de: tengo el gusto presentarles a nuestra directora||
Almost. The frame needs *de* before the verb: *tengo el gusto de*.
tengo el gusto de presento a nuestra directora||
Almost. After *de* the verb stays in its plain *-r* form, as English does with "to".
nos complace de invitarlos a la reunión||
Almost. *Nos complace* takes the dictionary form directly, with no *de*.
tengo gusto de invitarlos a la reunión||
Almost. The fixed phrase includes the little word *el*.
p:tener-en-cuenta: hay que tener cuenta el costo||
The *en* is part of the set phrase, so it can't be dropped.
hay que tener en cuenta hernando||
When what you take into account is a person, it needs *a*.
ten en cuenta de que cierran temprano||
A whole idea follows with just *que*, with no *de*.
p:tener-forma-de: la mesa es forma de corazón||
Almost. English says "is", but Spanish says the table *has* a shape, so use *tiene*.
la mesa tiene forma de redonda||
*De* is for nouns. An adjective like *redonda* goes straight after *forma*.
A noun after *forma* needs *de*, like "in the form of".
p:tener-ganas-de: English says going; after *de*, Spanish uses the dictionary form *salir*.
Don't drop the *de*: it links *ganas* to the verb.
p:tener-hambre: *Hambre* is a thing, not a description, so you have it: *tengo hambre*.
*Soy frío* means you're a cold person. Feeling cold is *tengo frío*.
*Muy* goes with describing words. *Hambre* is a thing, so you say how much of it: *mucha hambre*.
p:tener-la-mania-de: tienes la manía de revisando el celular||
Almost. English says 'in the habit of checking', but Spanish uses the dictionary form after *de*: *revisar*.
tienes manía de revisar el celular||
Keep the little word *la*: *la manía*, *la costumbre*, and *el vicio* for the bad habit.
estás en el hábito de llegar tarde||
English says "you're in the habit"; Spanish says you *have* it: *tienes la costumbre*.
p:tener-la-sensacion: me temo de que no va a llegar||
Almost. With *me temo*, go straight to *que*; the *de* belongs to the nouns like *sensación*.
me da la sensación de que nos esté escondiendo algo||
Almost. You believe it, so the verb stays ordinary: *está*.
tengo miedo que no va a llegar||
Almost. *Tengo miedo* is real fear; "I'm afraid that" in the polite sense is *me temo que*.
p:tener-lugar: la reunión tuvo un lugar el martes||
Almost. No *un* in this expression: *lugar* stays bare.
la reunión tomó lugar el martes||
English says "took place", but Spanish says "had place": *tener lugar*.
las protestas tuvo lugar en varias ciudades||
The verb matches the event, and there is more than one.
*Celebrarse* is only for planned events. A fire just *tiene lugar*.
p:tener-pensado-previsto: Almost. After *tener*, the word is the participle *pensado*, not the *-ando* form.
*Pensado* (the participle) is the word you need here.
p:tener-razon-pero: eres correcto pero no tenemos plata||
Almost. English says you *are* right, but Spanish says you *have* reason: *tienes razón*.
tienes muy razón pero altamira no va a esperar||
To stress it, use *toda la razón*, not *muy*.
A bare *pero* sounds like a flat no. Concede first, then push back.
p:tener-razon: That's English word for word. A person who's right *tiene razón*.
Almost. *Tú* takes *tienes*; *tiene* is for him, her or *usted*.
Hernando is *usted* to Tomás, so it's *usted tiene razón*.
p:tener-su-gracia: Almost. The little word agrees with the noun that follows: plural *riesgos* needs *sus*.
es su gracia que altamira hable de historia||
Almost. The phrase is built on *tener*, not *ser*.
Almost. *Los riesgos* is just "the risks"; *sus* adds the wry "quite a few".
p:tener-su-raiz-en: el conflicto tiene su raíz de la injusticia||
Almost. The cause comes after *en*, not *de*.
hay que cortar el problema de la raíz||
Almost. The fixed phrase is *de raíz*, with no article.
hay que cortar el problema en raíz||
Almost. English says "at the root", but Spanish uses *de*.
p:tengo-entendido-que: tengo entendido de que se aplazó la reunión||
Almost. Adding *de* here is a common slip, even among native speakers, but *tengo entendido* goes straight into *que*.
supe de vale que tomás se va||
Almost. For who told you, use *por*, not *de*.
Almost. You are reporting something you take as true, so no special mood: just *es*.
p:tengo-la-impresion-de-que: tengo la impresión de que sea tensa||
Almost. A hunch you believe takes the ordinary form, not the subjunctive.
Almost. Spanish says *la impresión de que*, with *la* and the *de*.
tengo la impresión de que el parque debe cerrar said to argue your case||
Almost. *Tengo la impresión* says you have no evidence, so don't use it for a claim you mean to defend.
p:tengo-miedo-de-que: Almost. English says *will come*, but after a fear Spanish uses the subjunctive, not the future.
tengo miedo de que perder a vale||
Almost. When you are the one afraid and the one losing, use the infinitive and no *que*.
Almost. *Preocupa* works like *gusta*: the worry bothers you, so *me* comes first.
p:tiene-mucha-luz: Almost. *Muchas luces* is lots of lamps; daylight is *mucha luz*.
Light is something the flat has, so *tiene*.
p:tienes-toda-la-razon: Almost. In Spanish you *have* reason, so the verb is *tener*.
Almost. *En absoluto* on its own always means *not at all*.
p:time-pasado-que-viene: *Pasado* comes after the time word; it's *próximo* that goes in front.
*Próxima* points forward, so the verb has to point forward too.
p:time-sequence-basic: Almost. *Primero* here means 'first of all' and never changes, even when a woman is speaking.
primero compro pan y abrí el café||luego
The order words don't make anything past; each verb needs its own past ending.
'First of all' doesn't go word for word. *Primero* on its own already says it.
p:todos-los-dias: Almost. Spanish keeps the *los* that English drops.
*Todo* matches the noun, so with *días* it's *todos*.
p:trabajar-de: Almost. *Como un mesero* sounds like he works the way a waiter does; for the job, use *de* with no article.
No *un* or *una* after *de*: the job stands alone.
*De* is for the job; for the place you work, use *en*.
p:traer-recuerdos: traigo recuerdos de mi abuela con el olor|yo|
Almost. The smell brings the memories, not you: put the smell as the subject.
One thing brings the memories, so the verb is singular.
su cara vino a la memoria||
Say who it came to mind for: *me*.
p:transport-en: English says by bus, but Spanish travels *en*: *en bus*, *en taxi*.
On foot is the one exception: *a pie*.
voy al trabajo en el bus||
*En el bus* points at one particular bus. For how you usually travel, drop the *el*.
p:tras-inf: Almost. English "after signing" uses the infinitive in Spanish, not the *-ando* form.
